Zenn の記事や本を VS Code、あるいは AI 統合エディタの Cursor で執筆するユーザー向けに、クリップボード内の画像をショートカットキー一発で貼り付けられる拡張機能「Zenn Image Paste」が公開された。Mac では Cmd+Alt+V、Windows では Ctrl+Alt+V を押すだけで、画像の保存と Markdown リンクの挿入がまとめて完了する点が特徴だ。

技術記事や同人誌を投稿できる Zenn は、GitHub リポジトリと連携してローカルで Markdown を編集する執筆スタイルを公式にサポートしている。専用の zenn-cli を使えば、手元のエディタで書いた内容をブラウザ上でプレビューしながら執筆できる。一方で、画像を扱う作業は手数が多い。スクリーンショットなどをいったんファイルとして保存し、所定の images フォルダへ配置したうえで、Markdown の画像記法を手書きする必要があり、執筆のテンポを損ねやすかった。

今回の拡張機能は、この一連の流れを自動化するものだ。クリップボードにコピーした画像をショートカットで貼り付けると、画像ファイルが適切な場所へ書き出され、同時にカーソル位置に対応する Markdown 記法が挿入される仕組みと見られる。Zenn のディレクトリ構成を前提に設計されているため、保存先の指定やパスの調整といった煩雑な操作を省ける点が利点になりそうだ。

画像貼り付けの支援自体は、VS Code 本体にも近年「Paste Image」に相当する機能が標準で備わりつつあり、関連する拡張機能も複数存在する。ただし、それらは汎用的な挙動が中心で、Zenn 特有のフォルダ規約やリンク形式に最適化されているとは限らない。特定のプラットフォームに合わせて細部を作り込んだツールには、執筆者の手間を確実に減らせる余地がある。

近年は Cursor をはじめ、VS Code をベースにした派生エディタや AI 補助機能の普及により、技術記事をローカル環境で書く人が増えている。こうした拡張機能は、日常的な執筆作業の小さな摩擦を取り除くものであり、同様にニッチな改善を狙ったツールが今後も登場する可能性がある。
7c8955bdea5a805c.bodyEn:
Writing technical articles often means peppering the text with screenshots, and few platforms make that workflow as Git-friendly, or as fiddly, as Zenn. A newly released Visual Studio Code extension called Zenn Image Paste aims to remove one of the most repetitive steps in that process: it lets authors paste an image from the clipboard directly into a Markdown file with a single keyboard shortcut, Cmd+Alt+V on macOS or Ctrl+Alt+V on Windows.

Zenn is a popular Japanese platform for publishing technical articles and books. Its distinguishing feature is a Git-based authoring model: instead of writing in a web editor, many authors use the official zenn-cli to compose Markdown locally, preview it in the browser, and publish by pushing to a connected GitHub repository. Images are stored as files inside an images directory in the repository and referenced from the Markdown with relative paths. This keeps content portable and version-controlled, but it also means that adding a screenshot normally involves several manual steps.

Without tooling, the typical sequence is to take a screenshot, save it to disk, move or rename the file into the project's images folder, and then type out the Markdown image syntax with the correct path. Repeating that for every figure in a long tutorial is tedious and error-prone, particularly when it comes to keeping file names unique and paths accurate. Zenn Image Paste appears to collapse all of that into one keystroke: copy an image to the clipboard, press the shortcut, and the extension writes the image file into the appropriate location and inserts the Markdown reference at the cursor.

The extension is explicitly positioned for both VS Code and Cursor. Cursor is an AI-focused code editor built as a fork of VS Code, which means it shares the same extension architecture and can run most VS Code extensions. Calling out Cursor support is increasingly common for new tooling, reflecting the editor's growing adoption among developers who also write about their work.

It is worth noting that VS Code already includes a built-in capability to paste or drag images into Markdown files, a feature that arrived in 2023. That native function copies the image into the workspace and inserts a Markdown link. A dedicated extension like Zenn Image Paste is likely valuable because it tailors the behavior to Zenn's specific conventions, such as the expected images directory structure, naming patterns, and the relative path format that Zenn's renderer expects. By binding the action to a distinct shortcut, it can also coexist with the editor's default paste behavior rather than overriding it.

For anyone unfamiliar with the broader ecosystem, the zenn-cli is the foundation of this local-first workflow. Authors typically run a command to scaffold a new article or book, which generates a Markdown file with front matter for metadata such as the title, an emoji, the type, and a published flag. The CLI also serves a live preview that mirrors how the content will look once published. Extensions that streamline editing, linting, or asset management slot naturally into that setup, and image pasting is one of the more obvious friction points to address.

The release fits a wider pattern of small, focused productivity tools built around content platforms and modern editors. As more developers maintain technical blogs alongside their code, utilities that shave seconds off routine actions can add up over the course of writing a detailed, image-heavy guide. The single-shortcut approach also lowers the barrier for newcomers who may not yet be comfortable with Zenn's directory layout.

As with any third-party extension, prospective users will want to confirm details such as where images are saved, how files are named, whether the path format matches their repository structure, and which image formats are supported. Those specifics determine how cleanly the tool drops into an existing project. For authors who frequently publish on Zenn from VS Code or Cursor, however, an extension that turns image insertion into a one-press operation is a practical, if narrowly scoped, convenience that targets a genuine and familiar pain point in the writing process.

c0e80c3aa5f7ccc1.bodyJa:
Chrome DevTools MCPは、AIエージェントが実際に動作しているChromeブラウザを直接操作し、その内部状態を検査できるようにするためのツールである。生成AIによるコーディング支援が一般化するなか、ブラウザ上の実挙動をAIに「見せる」手段を提供する点で、Web開発のデバッグ体験を変える可能性がある。

MCP(Model Context Protocol)は、AIモデルと外部ツールやデータソースをつなぐためのオープンな規格で、2024年にAnthropicが提唱した。対応するアプリケーション(MCPクライアント)からサーバーを介して、ファイル操作やAPI呼び出しといった機能を共通の作法で利用できる。Chrome DevTools MCPは、このサーバーの一つとして、Chrome開発チームが提供しているものだ。

従来、AIアシスタントが生成したコードがブラウザ上で意図通り動くかどうかは、人間が画面を確認してフィードバックする必要があった。Chrome DevTools MCPを導入すると、AI側がページへのアクセス、DOMの確認、コンソールのエラーログ取得、ネットワークリクエストの検査、パフォーマンス計測、スクリーンショット取得などをツールとして実行できる。つまりAIが自ら現象を観測し、修正案を検証する一連のループを回しやすくなる。

導入はNode.js環境を前提とし、npx経由でサーバーを起動する形が一般的だ。VS CodeのGitHub Copilotや、Claude、CursorといったMCPに対応する各種クライアントの設定ファイルにサーバー情報を追記することで利用できる。背後では、ブラウザ自動化で実績のあるChrome DevTools Protocol(CDP)やPuppeteer系の仕組みが使われているとされる。

同種の取り組みとしては、ブラウザ操作を担うPlaywright MCPなども登場しており、AIに「目」と「手」を与える流れは加速している。一方で、AIが任意のページにアクセスしたりコードを実行したりできる以上、認証情報の扱いや意図しない操作のリスクには注意が必要だ。検証用のプロファイルを分ける、扱う権限を絞るなど、運用面での配慮が求められる場面もあるだろう。記事の筆者が「幸福度が上がった」と表現するように開発体験の向上は期待できるが、導入効果は対象とするワークフローによって差が出ると見られる。
c0e80c3aa5f7ccc1.bodyEn:
Chrome DevTools MCP is an emerging way to give AI coding assistants direct, structured access to a live Chrome browser, and for many web developers it is changing how front-end debugging gets done. The tool exposes Chrome's debugging capabilities through the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets large language model agents call external tools in a consistent way. The practical upshot is that an AI assistant inside an editor such as Visual Studio Code can open a page, inspect what is happening, and reason about real browser behavior rather than guessing from source code alone.

To understand why this matters, it helps to recall what the Model Context Protocol is. MCP was introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 as a standardized interface between AI models and the outside world. Instead of every tool inventing its own integration, an MCP server advertises a set of capabilities, and any MCP-compatible client, including Claude Desktop, VS Code with GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and others, can call them. The protocol has since gained broad industry support, with major vendors shipping clients and servers, which is part of why a browser-focused server like this one slots in so easily.

Chrome DevTools MCP, published by the Chrome team, wraps the Chrome DevTools Protocol and the Puppeteer automation library behind that MCP interface. In concrete terms, it lets an agent perform tasks that previously required a human sitting in front of the DevTools panel. It can navigate to URLs, click and type to reproduce user flows, read the DOM and accessibility tree, capture screenshots, and pull console messages and network requests. It also surfaces performance tooling, so an agent can record a trace and report on metrics like Core Web Vitals. Because the agent sees actual runtime state, it can close the common gap where an assistant suggests a fix based on the code but never confirms whether the page actually behaves as expected.

Setup generally follows the same pattern as other MCP servers. The package is distributed through npm and is typically launched with a runner such as npx, then registered in the host application's MCP configuration. In VS Code, this means adding an entry that points to the server command so the assistant can discover the available browser tools. The Chrome team has positioned the project as relatively easy to adopt, and the main prerequisites are a recent Node.js installation and a Chrome binary the server can drive. As with any tool that automates a browser and reads page content, it is sensible to be mindful of what sites and credentials the agent is allowed to touch.

A typical workflow looks like this. A developer describes a bug, the assistant opens the affected page, reproduces the steps, reads the console for errors, and inspects the network panel for failed requests. It can then propose a code change and, after the change is applied, reload the page to verify the result. This loop of observe, hypothesize, fix, and confirm is what users tend to describe as the satisfying part, since it removes a lot of manual copying of error messages and back-and-forth context switching.

It is worth placing the tool in context, because it is not the only option. Microsoft maintains Playwright MCP, which similarly lets agents drive browsers across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, and there are several Puppeteer-based MCP servers as well. The distinction is largely one of emphasis. Playwright MCP leans toward cross-browser automation and testing scenarios, while Chrome DevTools MCP leans toward the inspection and diagnostic features that the DevTools panel is known for, such as performance traces and detailed console and network access. Which one fits best appears to depend on whether the priority is end-to-end test automation or deep debugging of a single Chromium-based target.

The broader trend here is the move from chat-only AI assistance toward agents that can act on real systems through standardized connectors. Browser access is a natural early target because so much development work is visual and stateful. None of this removes the need for developer judgment; the assistant can misread a page or propose an incorrect fix, and its observations are only as reliable as the tools it calls. Still, for the everyday grind of front-end debugging, a well-configured Chrome DevTools MCP setup can meaningfully shorten the feedback loop, which likely explains the enthusiastic reactions from those who have tried it.

7d9d6f0e93bf0452.bodyJa:
Visual Studio Code（VS Code）でGitHub Copilotとやり取りしたチャットのセッションが、ワークスペースの保存を忘れたまま閉じてしまったために見えなくなる——。こうしたトラブルに対処するため、Windows環境でセッションを復元するスクリプトが、QiitaのVS Code関連ブログで紹介された。

投稿者によれば、会社で約1か月にわたって続けていたCopilotとのやり取りが、ワークスペースを保存し忘れていたことで軒並み表示されなくなったという。これがスクリプトを作成した直接のきっかけとされる。前提はWindows PCでの開発で、対象は「保存を忘れてワークスペースを閉じてしまい、残しておきたかったセッション」を抱えるユーザーだ。

背景を補足すると、VS CodeはチャットやワークスペースごとのデータをユーザープロファイルのAppData配下などに保存する仕組みを持つ。Copilot Chatの履歴も内部的にはこうしたストレージへ書き出されると見られるが、ワークスペースを明示的に保存していない場合、再び開いた際にセッションとの関連付けがうまくたどれず、UI上から履歴が見えなくなる可能性がある。逆に言えば、ファイルとして残っているデータを探し出して読み込み直せれば、過去のやり取りを取り戻せる余地がある、という発想に基づくアプローチだ。

GitHub Copilotはコードのインライン補完だけでなく、Copilot Chatによる対話的な支援機能を備えており、近年はエージェント的な機能の拡充も進む。長い対話の文脈そのものが開発上の資産となるケースは増えており、セッションの消失は作業効率に直結しうる。VS Code側でもチャット履歴の管理機能は強化されてきているが、操作ミスや設定の行き違いで履歴を見失う状況は依然として起こり得る。

今回紹介されたようなスクリプトは公式機能ではなく、あくまで個人が自身の環境で動かした復旧手段である点には留意したい。ファイルの保存場所やフォーマットはVS CodeやCopilotのバージョン更新で変わる可能性があり、環境によってはそのまま動作しない場合もある。実行前にはデータのバックアップを取り、処理内容を理解したうえで利用することが望ましいだろう。
7d9d6f0e93bf0452.bodyEn:
Visual Studio Code's integration with GitHub Copilot has turned the chat panel into a working notebook where developers accumulate weeks of context, decisions, and iterative problem-solving, so losing that history can be a real setback. A recent Qiita blog post documents a small Windows-focused script built to recover Copilot chat sessions that became inaccessible after a workspace was closed without being saved, and it offers a useful window into where VS Code keeps this data and how it can sometimes be retrieved.

The author's motivation was concrete. About a month of conversations with Copilot at work stopped appearing in the interface because the workspace had never been explicitly saved as a .code-workspace file. In VS Code, chat sessions are associated with the context in which they were created. Opening a loose folder, an unsaved workspace, or a different combination of folders can change which stored sessions the editor links to the current window, so a conversation that was visible one day can appear to be gone the next even when the underlying files still exist on disk.

That distinction, between data that is genuinely deleted and data that is merely unlinked from the current view, is what makes recovery possible. On Windows, VS Code stores per-workspace state under the user's application data directory, typically beneath %APPDATA%\Code\User\workspaceStorage. Each workspace the editor has opened receives a subfolder identified by a hash, and inside these folders VS Code keeps state databases and JSON files, including chat history connected to Copilot. Because those files usually remain after a workspace is closed, the data is often still present; the difficulty lies in finding the right folder among many and reassociating it with a usable session.

The script described in the post appears to automate what is otherwise a tedious manual search. Instead of opening each hashed folder by hand, a script can enumerate the workspaceStorage subdirectories, read the relevant JSON, and surface candidate sessions so the wanted conversation can be identified and restored or copied out. On Windows this kind of task fits PowerShell well, since it can recursively scan directories, parse JSON natively, and filter results by timestamp or text content. The general technique is not specific to Copilot; similar approaches have long been used to recover other VS Code workspace state.

2bb8585e50446158.bodyJa:
AIコーディングのコスト管理というと、まずモデル名や1トークンあたりの料金表に目が向きがちだ。しかしAIエージェントが自律的にコードを書き進める「agentic coding」では、総コストを左右するのは1回の応答単価よりも、エージェントがどう試行を繰り返すかという「ループ設計」だという指摘が出ている。

従来のチャット型AI利用では、ユーザーが質問しAIが一度答える、という単発のやり取りが基本だった。この場合、コストは「使ったモデル × やり取り回数」でおおむね見積もれる。だから高価なモデルを軽量モデルに替えれば素直に安くなる、という直感が成り立ちやすい。

一方、agentic codingではAIエージェントが自らタスクを分解し、ファイルを読み、コードを書き、テストを実行し、エラーを見て修正する、という一連の動作をループとして繰り返す。GitHub Copilotのエージェントモードや、Claude Code、CursorやClineといったツールはいずれもこの方式を採る。ここで問題になるのは、1回のループで処理しきれない場合にエージェントが何度も同じ文脈を読み直し、トークン消費が雪だるま式に膨らむ点だ。

つまり、たとえ単価の安いモデルを選んでも、タスクの与え方やコンテキストの渡し方が悪くループ回数が増えれば、総額はかえって高くつく可能性がある。逆に高性能モデルでも、1〜2回で正解にたどり着けるよう設計すれば、結果的に安く済むこともある。

コストを抑える鍵として挙げられるのは、エージェントに渡す指示やコンテキストを絞り込んで無駄な再読み込みを減らすこと、適切な粒度でタスクを区切ること、そして失敗ループが延々と続かないよう停止条件を設けることなどだ。プロンプトキャッシュや差分のみを渡す工夫も有効と見られる。

モデルの世代交代が続くなかで料金は今後も変動するが、開発現場で見るべきはカタログ上の単価だけではない。エージェントがどれだけ効率よく目的に到達するか、そのループの設計こそが、実運用のコストと開発体験を大きく左右する要素になりつつあると言えそうだ。
2bb8585e50446158.bodyEn:
When teams estimate the cost of AI-assisted development, the first instinct is to look at the model and its price per token. A capable frontier model looks expensive, a smaller model looks cheap, and the conclusion seems obvious: switch to the lighter option to save money. In the era of agentic coding, that reasoning is incomplete and sometimes misleading. The dominant cost driver is usually not the sticker price of a single response but the design of the loop that the agent runs to reach a result.

An agentic coding tool does not answer once and stop. It operates in a cycle: it reads the task, inspects files, calls tools, runs tests or commands, observes the output, and decides what to do next. This pattern, often described as a reason-and-act loop, repeats until the agent believes the task is done or a limit is reached. Each turn sends the accumulated conversation — instructions, prior tool outputs, file contents, error messages — back to the model. Because the context grows with every step, token usage tends to compound rather than stay flat.

This is where the arithmetic shifts. A model with a low per-token price that needs twenty iterations, each carrying a large and growing context, can easily cost more than a more expensive model that completes the same task in three focused steps. The number of loop iterations, the size of the context carried between them, and how often the agent retries after failures often matter more than the headline rate. A cheaper model that reasons less reliably may also loop more, partly offsetting or even reversing the expected savings.

Several factors inflate the loop. Large file reads dumped into context, verbose tool output, repeated re-reading of the same files, and unclear stop conditions all add turns and tokens. Failure handling is particularly sensitive: if a model misreads an error and tries several wrong fixes, every attempt pays the full context cost again. Poorly scoped tasks compound this, because an agent given a vague goal explores more before it converges.

This dynamic is visible across the current generation of tools, including GitHub Copilot's agent mode, Cursor, Claude Code, Aider, and more autonomous systems such as Devin. They differ in interface but share the same underlying loop, so their running costs depend heavily on how that loop is orchestrated rather than only on the model behind it. Vendors have responded with mechanisms aimed squarely at loop economics. Prompt caching, offered by providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, lets repeated prefixes such as system prompts and stable context be billed at a reduced rate, which directly targets the repetition inherent in loops. Context compaction, summarization of earlier turns, and subagent patterns that isolate work into smaller contexts pursue the same goal from the application side.

For teams, the practical implication is that cost control belongs in loop design. Limiting unnecessary iterations, giving the agent precise scopes and clear completion criteria, trimming what gets pulled into context, using retrieval instead of wholesale file dumps, and enabling caching tend to influence the bill more than swapping models alone. Observability helps here. Tracking tokens per task, iterations per task, and retry rates makes the real drivers visible, since a per-response price tells only part of the story.

None of this means model choice is irrelevant. A stronger model that solves a task in fewer, cleaner steps can be the cheaper option overall, while a weaker model may be appropriate for narrow, well-defined work. There are also second-order effects, such as a faster model reducing wall-clock time and human waiting, that a token table does not capture. The point is that in agentic workflows the model is one variable inside a larger system. The cost of building with AI agents appears to be determined less by which name sits at the top of the pricing page and more by how the surrounding loop is engineered, measured, and constrained.

962aef109ae95dda.bodyJa:
在宅ワークのデスク環境を客観的に評価したい——そんな素朴な疑問に応えるため、デスクの写真を1枚アップロードするだけでAIが椅子・モニター・照明など8項目を100点満点で採点するWebツールが個人開発者によって公開された。画像と言語を結びつけるモデル「CLIP」を用い、Hugging Faceの無料枠で動作する点が特徴だ。

中核となるCLIP（Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training）は、米OpenAIが2021年に公開した画像・テキストの対照学習モデルである。大量の画像とキャプションの組を学習することで、画像と任意のテキストの「意味的な近さ」を数値化できる。これにより、分類カテゴリを事前に学習していなくても、「整理されたデスク」「明るい照明」といった説明文と写真の類似度を計算する、いわゆるゼロショット推論が可能になる。

このツールはおそらく、各評価項目に対応するポジティブ・ネガティブな説明文を用意し、アップロード画像との類似度スコアを100点満点に換算していると見られる。学習済みの分類器を新たに用意する必要がなく、プロンプト（説明文）の工夫だけで採点軸を定義できるため、個人開発でも短期間で形にしやすい。

動作環境にはHugging Face Spacesの無料枠が使われている。Spacesはデモアプリを手軽に公開できるホスティングサービスで、PythonベースのUIフレームワークGradioやStreamlitと組み合わせれば、サーバー管理の知識が乏しくてもブラウザで動くアプリを構築できる。無料枠はCPU中心で処理速度に制約はあるものの、CLIP程度の推論であれば実用的に動くケースが多い。

CLIPを応用した採点・検索ツールは近年増えており、画像検索や自動タグ付け、コンテンツのモデレーションなどにも使われている。一方で、採点結果はモデルの学習データや説明文の設計に左右されるため、人間の美的感覚や個別の用途を厳密に反映するものではない点には留意が必要だ。それでも、最新の生成AIに頼らずとも既存のオープンモデルと無料インフラを組み合わせるだけで、遊び心のある実用ツールを作れることを示す好例と言えそうだ。
962aef109ae95dda.bodyEn:
A developer has published a web tool that uses OpenAI's CLIP model to rate photographs of home-office desks, assigning a score out of 100 across eight categories such as chair, monitor and lighting. Described in a Zenn blog post, the project began from a simple personal question—how good is my remote-work setup, objectively?—and turns it into a compact demonstration of how a multimodal model can be repurposed for a casual, subjective-feeling task without any custom training, and hosted entirely on a free tier.

The appeal is twofold. For anyone curious about their own workspace, the tool offers a quick, gamified critique from uploading a single image. For developers, it is a small but instructive case study in deploying a vision-language model on no-cost infrastructure, the kind of weekend build that lowers the barrier to experimenting with image understanding.

CLIP, short for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training, was released by OpenAI in early 2021. It was trained on a large collection of image-text pairs gathered from the web, learning to map pictures and their textual descriptions into a shared embedding space. The practical consequence is so-called zero-shot classification: instead of training a dedicated classifier for every label, you supply candidate text prompts and ask the model which one best matches a given image. This flexibility is what makes a project like a desk scorer feasible for an individual, because no labeled dataset of "good" and "bad" desks needs to be assembled.

In practice, the scoring approach likely works by phrasing each evaluation dimension as competing text prompts—for example "a desk with excellent lighting" versus "a desk with poor lighting"—and measuring the similarity between the uploaded image's embedding and each prompt's embedding. The relative similarity can then be normalized into a figure on a 0-100 scale. Repeating this across eight axes produces a category-by-category breakdown rather than a single opaque number, which appears to be part of the tool's presentation.

It is worth being clear about what such a score represents. CLIP's outputs reflect statistical associations learned from its training data, not a calibrated or expert aesthetic judgment, so the numbers should be read as a playful heuristic rather than an authoritative verdict. Results may also lean toward whatever desk styles and photographic conventions were common online, and the model can be sensitive to lighting, angle and image quality. The "100-point" framing is a presentation convention layered on top of similarity scores, and small prompt changes can shift the outcome noticeably.

The hosting choice is central to the project's accessibility. Hugging Face Spaces offers a free tier for hosting small demos, commonly built with lightweight Python interface frameworks such as Gradio or Streamlit, which handle the file upload and result display with minimal code. The free CPU allocation is limited in memory and compute, but a CLIP inference pass on a single image is modest enough to run within those constraints, which is likely why the model and deployment target fit together well for this kind of demo.

For context, CLIP is no longer the only option for this style of task, and the surrounding ecosystem has expanded considerably. OpenCLIP provides community-trained open weights at various scales, while Google's SigLIP uses a different training objective and is often cited for improved efficiency and accuracy on zero-shot benchmarks. For richer, descriptive feedback rather than similarity scores, captioning and visual question-answering models such as BLIP, or larger vision-language systems like LLaVA and commercial multimodal APIs, can generate written assessments of an image. A builder could, in principle, swap CLIP for one of these to produce explanations alongside the numeric ratings, at the cost of greater compute.

As a piece of engineering, the desk scorer is intentionally modest, but it illustrates a broader trend: capable pretrained models combined with free or low-cost hosting let individuals ship interactive AI demos quickly. The same pattern—pair a zero-shot vision model with simple prompts and a web front end—can be adapted to many lightweight rating or sorting tasks. Readers interested in trying it can run their own image through the live demo, while treating the resulting score as entertainment and a starting point for tinkering rather than a definitive measure of their workspace.

7e1f61313e3cbf1d.bodyJa:
ローカルで動かす大規模言語モデル（LLM）を使い、GitHub Copilot 向けに開発したスキルの品質評価（eval）を行う――そんな試みの過程で直面した課題が、開発ツール「isdd」の v1.0.14 開発ログとして公開された。クラウド依存を避けつつ AI コーディング支援の評価を自動化したい開発者にとって、参考になる知見と言える。

isdd（Interview-driven Spec-driven Development）は、GitHub Copilot のスキル機能を活用し、要件定義から詳細設計、実装までを一貫した ID で追跡できるようにする仕組みである。仕様駆動開発（Spec-driven Development）の考え方を取り入れ、対話（インタビュー）を通じて仕様を固めていく点が特徴とされる。近年は GitHub の Spec Kit など、仕様を起点に AI へ実装を委ねるアプローチが各所で模索されており、isdd もその系譜に位置づけられる。

今回の開発ログで焦点となっているのは、こうしたスキルの挙動を検証する「eval」をローカル LLM で実行する際の難しさだ。eval とは、モデルやプロンプトの出力が期待どおりかを自動で判定する評価工程を指す。クラウドの高性能モデルではなくローカルモデルを用いる背景には、コスト削減やプライバシー確保、再現性の高い検証環境を求める狙いがあると見られる。

一方で、ローカル環境ならではのハマりどころも少なくない。記事では、モデルの応答形式や出力の揺らぎ、評価スクリプトとの連携など、実行にこぎ着けるまでに調整を要した点が具体的に振り返られているもようだ。ローカル LLM の実行には Ollama や LM Studio、llama.cpp といった基盤が広く使われるが、モデルごとに対応する形式やコンテキスト長が異なり、クラウド API と同じ感覚では動かしにくい場面がある。

AI コーディング支援の分野では、Copilot に加えて Cursor や各種エージェント型ツールが台頭し、出力品質をどう客観的に測るかが共通の課題となっている。今回のような開発ログは、個人やチームが自前で評価基盤を整える際の実践的な手がかりになる可能性がある。ローカル LLM の性能向上が続くなか、こうした検証の試みは今後さらに増えていくと考えられる。
7e1f61313e3cbf1d.bodyEn:
isdd, short for Interview-driven Spec-driven Development, is a workflow that leans on GitHub Copilot's skill feature to keep requirements definition, detailed design, and implementation linked together through consistent identifiers. The development log for version 1.0.14 turns to a narrower but increasingly relevant goal: running automated evaluations, often called "evals," of those Copilot skills against a locally hosted large language model rather than a cloud endpoint. The exercise matters because reproducible, low-cost evaluation is quickly becoming a prerequisite for anyone shipping LLM-driven developer tooling, and local inference removes both per-token billing and data-handling concerns from the testing loop.

The core idea behind an eval is straightforward: feed a model a set of fixed inputs, capture its outputs, and score them against expected results or rubric-based criteria. For a system like isdd, where each skill is meant to move a project from interview notes to a specification and then to traceable implementation tasks, evals are the only practical way to confirm that a change to a prompt or skill definition does not silently degrade behavior. Doing this against a local model also lets the author iterate quickly without rate limits, which is a common motivation cited across the local-LLM community.

A recurring source of friction, according to the log, appears to be the gap between how GitHub Copilot's hosted environment expects skills to behave and how a self-hosted model responds to the same instructions. Copilot skills are typically designed around a specific interaction contract, and smaller local models do not always follow structured-output expectations as reliably as the larger commercial models they are being compared against. When a skill expects a particular JSON shape or an ID-tagged response, a model that drifts from that format can cause the whole evaluation pipeline to fail before any meaningful scoring happens.

Wiring a local model into tooling built for Copilot is the other obvious hurdle. Most local runtimes, such as Ollama, LM Studio, and llama.cpp-based servers, now expose an OpenAI-compatible API, which in principle lets existing clients point at a localhost address instead of a vendor endpoint. In practice, the compatibility is partial. Differences in how tool or function calling is supported, how system prompts are templated, and how context windows are handled can all surface as confusing errors. The log's framing around "what I got stuck on" suggests these integration mismatches, rather than the modeling itself, consumed much of the effort.

Context length and prompt formatting are likely contributors as well. Spec-driven workflows tend to accumulate long documents, interview transcripts, design notes, and prior IDs, and feeding that history into a model with a limited context window can lead to truncation or degraded reasoning. Each model family also has its own chat template and stop tokens, so a prompt that works cleanly through Copilot may need adjustment before a local model produces comparable output. Determinism is a related concern: evals are most useful when runs are repeatable, which usually means pinning temperature, seeds where available, and model versions so that score changes can be attributed to deliberate edits rather than sampling noise.

For readers approaching this space, a few adjacent concepts are worth knowing. Spec-driven development has gained visibility through tools and patterns that treat written specifications as the source of truth for code generation, and GitHub's own moves toward customizable Copilot behavior, including custom instructions and skills, sit alongside this trend. On the evaluation side, frameworks such as promptfoo, OpenAI's evals format, and various LLM-as-judge approaches provide reusable scaffolding, while local-first inference is supported by a growing ecosystem of quantized open-weight models that run on consumer hardware.

The broader takeaway from the v1.0.14 log is less about a single breakthrough and more about the maturing practice of testing LLM features the way other software is tested. Treating Copilot skills as components that deserve regression checks, and choosing a local model to make those checks cheap and private, reflects a pragmatic direction many small projects appear to be taking. The struggles documented here, primarily around output formatting, API compatibility, and reproducibility, are likely to be familiar to anyone attempting a similar setup, which is what makes a development log of this kind useful beyond its own codebase.

836ffb5bdae333c1.bodyJa:
検証環境のデータベースからデータを取り出し、手元のPCに持ち込む――開発の現場では時折発生する地味な作業を、AIに任せてみたという検証記事が公開された。単純に見えて実際にはネットワーク構成の制約が絡むため意外と手間がかかる作業であり、こうした定型的だが煩雑なタスクをAIがどこまで肩代わりできるかを示す一例として興味深い。

題材となったのは、AWSのRDS上で稼働するPostgreSQLである。RDSはVPC(仮想プライベートネットワーク)の内側に置かれているため、ローカルPCから直接接続することはできない。一般的には踏み台サーバー(bastion host)を経由したSSHトンネルや、AWS Systems Managerのセッションマネージャーによるポートフォワーディングを用いて、安全に接続経路を確立する必要がある。その上でpg_dumpなどのツールでデータをエクスポートし、ローカルに取り込むという手順を踏むことになる。

こうした作業は、コマンドのオプションや認証情報、接続先の指定といった細かな点でつまずきやすい。記事では、AIにこの一連の流れを指示し実行させる試みが紹介されているとみられる。近年はターミナル操作やファイル編集を伴う作業をAIに委ねる「AIエージェント」型のツールが広がっており、Claude CodeやCursor、各種CLIツールなどが代表例として挙げられる。

カテゴリが「local-llm」とされている点からは、クラウドのAPIではなくローカル環境で動作する言語モデルの活用も視野に入っている可能性がある。ローカルLLMはデータが外部に送られにくいという利点があり、DBの接続情報や実データを扱う場面ではセキュリティ上の安心感につながりやすい。一方で、クラウド型の大規模モデルと比べると推論精度や対応力で差が出る場合もあり、用途に応じた使い分けが求められる。

このような取り組みは、インフラ周りの定型作業を自動化・省力化する流れの一端を示すものといえる。AIがどこまで正確に手順を遂行できるか、また誤操作やデータ漏えいをどう防ぐかは引き続き課題となるが、日常的な開発作業の効率化に向けた実践例として参考になりそうだ。
836ffb5bdae333c1.bodyEn:
Exporting database data from a staging environment and copying it down to a local machine is the kind of unglamorous chore that surfaces only occasionally, yet tends to consume more time than expected each time it comes up. A recent post on Zenn documents one developer's attempt to hand this task to an AI assistant rather than work through every step manually, and it offers a useful window into how agentic AI tooling is being applied to ordinary infrastructure work.

The friction in this case stems largely from the environment's network topology. The PostgreSQL database runs on Amazon RDS and sits inside a VPC, which means it is not directly reachable from a developer's laptop. Reaching it generally requires establishing a path through the isolation boundary first. Common approaches include opening an SSH tunnel through a bastion host, or using port forwarding via AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager, which avoids exposing a public SSH endpoint. Only once that connection exists can an export tool actually talk to the database, so the apparent simplicity of "just grab the data" hides several setup steps that are easy to get wrong.

After connectivity is in place, the extraction itself typically relies on pg_dump or a comparable utility. The operator has to supply the correct host, port, database name, and credentials, choose an appropriate dump format such as plain SQL or PostgreSQL's custom compressed format, and then move the resulting file to the local machine. Frequently the workflow does not end there: the dump is restored into a local PostgreSQL instance with pg_restore or psql so the data can be queried and tested offline. None of these individual commands is difficult, but stringing them together correctly, with the right flags and the right order, is exactly the sort of repetitive, error-prone sequence that people would rather not redo from memory.

This is where an AI agent fits in. Modern coding assistants can be given a high-level goal and then allowed to execute shell commands, read the output, and adjust their next step accordingly. In practice that means the assistant can attempt to open the tunnel, run the dump, detect failures such as authentication errors or missing flags, and retry. The article's framing under the "local-llm" category suggests the author was interested in using a locally run model, which is a notable detail given that the task touches database credentials and potentially sensitive data. Keeping the model on-device, rather than sending command output and connection details to a hosted service, appears to be part of the appeal, although the post's exact setup would determine how fully that privacy benefit is realized.

The broader context is the rapid maturation of agentic developer tools. Assistants such as Claude Code, Aider, Cline, and similar terminal-oriented agents have made it increasingly common to delegate multi-step operational tasks rather than only code generation. At the same time, locally hosted models served through runtimes like Ollama or LM Studio have lowered the barrier to running capable open-weight models on a workstation. Combining the two is an emerging pattern: an agent loop driven by a model that never leaves the machine. How well a local model performs on this kind of work is likely to vary, since smaller models can struggle with the precise syntax of tools like pg_dump and AWS CLI compared with larger hosted counterparts.

Several caveats are worth keeping in mind for anyone considering a similar approach. Allowing an AI to execute commands against real infrastructure carries obvious risks, so guardrails such as read-only credentials, confirmation prompts before destructive actions, and a non-production target are prudent. Staging data may still contain personal information, which means handling it locally does not automatically remove compliance obligations. And because the agent can confidently produce plausible but incorrect commands, reviewing what it runs remains essential.

Ultimately the experiment reads less as a claim that AI has solved database operations and more as a practical illustration of where these tools currently help. For recurring, well-bounded chores that nonetheless require fiddly setup, delegating the mechanics to an assistant can reduce friction, provided a human stays in the loop to verify the results.

de0678145a0f4241.bodyJa:
The Atlantic記者のAlex Reisner氏が、生成AIの学習に利用されているとみられる音楽データセット4件を発見し、誰でも検索できる形で一般に公開した。AIによる楽曲生成サービスが急速に広がるなか、学習データの中身がほとんど明らかにされてこなかった現状に光を当てる取り組みとして注目される。

報道によると、発見された4件のうち2件は1200万件を超える規模に達する大規模なデータセットだという。アーティストやリスナーは公開された検索ツールを通じて、特定の楽曲や演奏者が学習用データに含まれているかどうかを自分で確かめられる。これにより、これまで開発企業側しか把握していなかった情報の一部が、権利者や一般の利用者にも開かれることになる。

生成AIの分野では、モデルがどのようなデータで訓練されたのかという「学習データの透明性」が大きな論点になっている。Reisner氏は以前にも、大規模言語モデルの学習に使われた書籍データセット(いわゆる「Books3」など)を検索可能にする調査報道を手がけており、今回の音楽版はその延長線上にある取り組みと位置づけられる。

音楽をめぐっては、SunoやUdioといったAI楽曲生成サービスに対し、大手レコード会社が著作権侵害を主張して訴訟を起こすなど、権利処理をめぐる緊張が高まっている。学習データに自身の楽曲が含まれているかを確認できる手段が乏しいことは、権利者が侵害の有無を判断するうえでの障壁になってきた。今回のデータベースは、そうした検証作業を後押しする可能性がある。

一方で、データセットに楽曲が含まれていること自体が、ただちに違法な利用や著作権侵害を意味するわけではない点には注意が必要だ。フェアユースなどの法的評価は国や状況によって異なり、現在も各地で係争中の論点が多い。それでも、これまでブラックボックス化していた学習データの一端が可視化される意義は小さくなく、AI開発における透明性や説明責任を求める議論をさらに加速させると見られる。
de0678145a0f4241.bodyEn:
The Atlantic has published a searchable database of music recordings that appear to have been used to train artificial intelligence models, offering the public a rare look at the raw material feeding a fast-growing category of generative tools. The project was assembled by reporter Alex Reisner, who says he uncovered four separate datasets, two of which are described as enormous, each containing more than 12 million entries. The release matters because the question of what music goes into AI systems sits at the center of mounting legal and ethical disputes between technology companies and the people who create and own recorded music.

According to the reporting, the datasets vary in size and composition, but the two largest stand out for their scale, suggesting that the models trained on them may have ingested a substantial cross-section of recorded music. By making the collections fully searchable, The Atlantic allows artists, songwriters, rights holders, and ordinary listeners to check whether specific works appear in the underlying data. That kind of direct lookup is significant because AI developers rarely disclose the contents of their training sets in detail, often citing competitive concerns or describing their sources only in broad terms such as "publicly available" or "licensed" material.

This is not Reisner's first effort of this kind. He previously built searchable tools for The Atlantic exposing collections of books used to train large language models, including datasets drawn from pirated text repositories. Those earlier projects helped authors discover that their work had been swept into AI training without permission, and they fueled wider scrutiny of how foundation models are built. Applying the same approach to music extends that line of investigation into an industry that has its own deeply established licensing norms and powerful rights-holding institutions.

The timing aligns with intensifying conflict over generative music tools. Companies such as Suno and Udio have drawn attention for systems that can produce full songs from short text prompts, and they have faced litigation from major record labels and industry groups alleging that their models were trained on copyrighted recordings without authorization. The companies have generally defended their practices, with arguments that often invoke fair use or transformative use, while rights holders contend that wholesale copying of recordings to build commercial products falls outside those protections. A publicly searchable database does not resolve those legal questions, but it can provide concrete evidence about what material is involved, which is frequently the hardest thing for outside parties to establish.

Transparency around training data has become one of the defining debates in AI policy. Critics argue that without visibility into datasets, creators cannot know whether their work was used, regulators cannot assess compliance, and the public cannot evaluate claims made by developers. Supporters of disclosure point to emerging requirements, such as provisions in the European Union's AI Act that call for summaries of training content, as a direction the industry may increasingly be pushed toward. Tools like The Atlantic's database operate in that gap, surfacing information that companies have been reluctant to volunteer.

It is worth noting some limits to what such a resource can show. The presence of a track in a dataset does not by itself prove that a particular commercial model was trained on it, nor does it establish how the data was obtained or whether any licensing was in place. Datasets can be compiled, copied, and circulated among researchers in ways that are difficult to trace back to a specific product. Readers examining the database are therefore likely to find strong signals about industry practices rather than definitive proof about any single company's choices.

Even with those caveats, the publication adds to a growing body of independent reporting that aims to make AI training practices legible to the people most affected by them. For musicians and labels weighing whether to pursue licensing deals, opt-out mechanisms, or litigation, the ability to search for their own catalog provides a starting point. More broadly, the project reflects a shift in which journalists and researchers, rather than the AI developers themselves, are increasingly the ones documenting what these systems are built from.

8d89bac5ec6a16f3.bodyJa:
ローカルLLM環境でRTX 4070のような中位GPUを使う場合、新しいモデルの「速さ」は単純なベンチマーク値だけでは判断できない。Qiitaに投稿された検証記事は、新世代の「Qwen3.6」を4070で動かした際、当初は前世代のおよそ半分の速度に見えたものの、その原因がモデル本体ではなく実行構成にあったと報告している。

Qwenは中国・アリババが開発するオープンモデル群で、近年はMoE(Mixture of Experts、混合エキスパート)構成を採用した版が注目を集めている。筆者はここ数日、35B規模のQwenをローカルで追い続けてきたが、鍵となったのはこのMoE構成における推論処理の割り当て方だった。エキスパート層をあえてCPU側に追い出し、注意機構や共有層をGPUに残す構成へ切り替えたところ、速度は約2.8倍に向上し、34.6 tok/sに達したという。

この挙動は一見直感に反するが、MoEの特性を踏まえると理解しやすい。エキスパート層はトークンごとに一部しか活性化されないため、VRAMが限られる環境では、全層をGPUに詰め込んで容量を圧迫するより、疎にしか使われない部分をCPUへ逃がすほうが全体のスループットが上がる場合がある。つまり「前世代の半速」という第一印象は、モデルの実力ではなく、デフォルト寄りの割り当てがボトルネックになっていた可能性が高い。

性能面でも、筆者が用いる標準的な7問のテストでは7問すべてに正解し、さらにコーディングエージェントのバックエンドとしても実用に足ると評価している。量子化と適切なオフロードを組み合わせれば、12GB級のGPUでも35B級モデルを現実的な速度で扱えることを示す一例といえる。

llama.cppやvLLMなど、CPUとGPUをまたぐオフロードを細かく制御できるツールが普及したことも、こうした最適化を後押ししている。同種の手法は他のMoE系オープンモデルにも応用できると見られ、限られたハードウェアでローカル推論を行うユーザーにとって、構成チューニングの重要性を改めて示す事例だろう。
8d89bac5ec6a16f3.bodyEn:
Running capable large language models on consumer graphics cards remains one of the most active corners of the local AI community, and a recent hands-on writeup highlights why careful configuration can matter as much as the model itself. Over several days, the author benchmarked a new-generation Qwen model in the roughly 35-billion-parameter class on an RTX 4070, a mainstream GPU with 12GB of video memory. An initial test made the model look like it ran at about half the speed of the previous generation. On closer inspection, however, the bottleneck appeared to come not from the model's design but from how its weights were distributed between the GPU and the rest of the system.

The crucial detail is the model's architecture. Recent Qwen releases include Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants, in which a routing mechanism activates only a small subset of the network's "experts" for each token. That means the total parameter count can be large while the compute and memory touched per token stays comparatively small. For anyone trying to fit such a model onto a 12GB card, the implication is significant: not every part of the network is equally hot, so where each tensor lives has an outsized effect on speed.

This is where the offloading strategy comes in. With a 35B-class model, the weights cannot all fit in 12GB at useful quantization levels, so some portion must spill to system RAM and run on the CPU. A naive approach splits the network layer by layer, which can inadvertently leave latency-sensitive components on the slower side of the divide. The reported fix was to deliberately keep the always-active parts, attention and the shared layers, on the GPU while pushing the large, sparsely used expert weights out to the CPU. Because those experts are only occasionally invoked per token, the penalty for running them on the CPU is smaller than it might first appear.

According to the report, that change was decisive. Targeted expert offloading raised throughput by about 2.8 times, reaching 34.6 tokens per second. For interactive use on a single mainstream GPU, that figure is comfortably in the range where a chat or coding workflow feels responsive rather than sluggish. The headline takeaway is therefore less about a regression in the new model and more about the importance of matching the loader's configuration to an MoE architecture.

Tools such as llama.cpp make this kind of fine-grained control possible. Its tensor-override options let users specify which tensors are kept on the GPU and which are sent to the CPU, rather than relying solely on a coarse layer count. Quantized GGUF weights, combined with that selective placement, are what allow a model of this size to run at all on 12GB. Front-ends and runners like Ollama and LM Studio build on similar foundations, though the most aggressive expert-offloading tricks typically require dropping down to the underlying flags.

Speed is only half the story. The author also reports that the configuration scored 7 out of 7 on a personal set of seven standard questions, suggesting the quantized, partially offloaded

4dab75911dad6505.bodyJa:
プログラミング経験がなく、英語のドキュメントもほとんど読めない会社員が、AIコードエディタ「Cursor」だけを使って診断系のWebアプリを2本公開した――。Zennで公開された個人ブログが、AIによる開発の裾野がどこまで広がりつつあるかを示す一例として共有されている。

筆者によれば、開発にあてた時間は平日の夜と日曜のみ。やったことは大きく三つで、Cursorに日本語で指示を出し、生成されたファイルの内容を確認し、デプロイ(公開作業)の手順をコピー&ペーストするというものだ。コードを自力で書くのではなく、AIに作らせて動かすという進め方が、専門知識のない個人でも形になりうることを体現している。

Cursorは、マイクロソフトのコードエディタ「VS Code」をベースに開発されたAI統合型エディタで、大規模言語モデル(LLM)を使い自然言語の指示からコードを生成・修正できる。チャット形式でやり取りしながらエラーの原因を尋ねたり、ファイル全体を書き換えさせたりできる点が特徴だ。日本語での指示にも対応しているため、英語が苦手なユーザーでも扱いやすいと見られる。

こうした「自然言語でアプリを作る」流れは、近年「バイブコーディング(vibe coding)」とも呼ばれ関心が高まっている。CursorのほかにもGitHubの「Copilot」、Anthropicの「Claude Code」、Codeiumの「Windsurf」など競合は多く、画面イメージから素早く試作品を作るVercelの「v0」や「Bolt.new」といったサービスも登場した。公開先としても、VercelやNetlifyなど初心者が比較的扱いやすい基盤が整ってきている。

一方で、AI任せの開発には注意点もある。生成されたコードの安全性や品質を本人が十分に検証できない場合、不具合や情報漏えいなどのリスクを見落とす可能性は残る。今回の事例も、あくまで個人が短期間で公開までこぎ着けたという一例であり、誰もが同じ成果を得られるとは限らない。それでも、専門教育を受けていない人が「作りたいもの」を自分の手で形にできる環境が広がりつつあることを示す、象徴的な報告と言えそうだ。
4dab75911dad6505.bodyEn:
A blog post published on Zenn describes how an office worker with no prior coding experience and limited English reading ability built and released two "diagnostic" web apps using only Cursor, working in the evenings on weekdays and on Sundays. The account matters because it illustrates, in concrete terms, how AI-assisted development tools are lowering the barrier to entry for people who would previously have been unable to ship working software at all.

According to the author, the workflow was strikingly narrow. Rather than learning a programming language or studying framework documentation, the person issued instructions to Cursor in Japanese, reviewed the files the tool generated, and then copied and pasted the deployment steps it provided. The "diagnostic" apps in question are the quiz-style personality or compatibility tests that are popular in Japan, where a user answers a series of questions and receives a categorized result. Such apps are a reasonable starting point for a beginner because the core logic, scoring answers and mapping them to outcomes, is relatively self-contained, and the user interface can be kept simple.

Cursor is an AI-centric code editor built as a fork of Microsoft's Visual Studio Code. It integrates large language models directly into the editing environment, allowing users to describe what they want in natural language and receive generated or modified code in return. Features such as inline editing, a chat panel that can read the open project, and an "agent" mode that can plan and apply changes across multiple files are central to its appeal. For a non-programmer, the significant point is that the tool can operate on the whole project context, so a vague request in plain language can be turned into concrete files without the user needing to know where each piece belongs.

The fact that the author works only on weeknights and Sundays underscores a broader shift. Building a small web application has historically required familiarity with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, a framework, version control, and a hosting setup, a combination that typically takes months to learn. When the model handles the translation from intent to code, the remaining tasks become checking whether the result looks correct and following deployment instructions step by step. The author's description suggests that the harder part may now be verification and iteration rather than initial authoring, since a beginner still has to recognize when something is wrong and ask for a fix.

This case sits within a fast-moving category often described as "vibe coding," a term popularized in early 2025 to describe building software primarily by prompting an AI and accepting its output. Cursor competes with several adjacent tools. GitHub Copilot pioneered in-editor AI suggestions; Windsurf offers a similar agentic editor; and browser-based products such as Replit, Vercel's v0, Bolt, and Lovable let users generate and preview apps without installing anything locally. Underneath, these tools rely on frontier models from providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, and the quality of generated code has improved markedly as those models have advanced.

Deployment, the step the author reportedly reduced to copy-and-paste, has likewise become more accessible. Platforms such as Vercel and Netlify can take a project from a repository and publish it to a public URL with minimal configuration, handling build steps and hosting automatically. Combined with an AI editor that writes the deployment commands, this removes one of the traditional stumbling blocks for newcomers.

Some caveats are worth noting. An app that works is not necessarily secure, maintainable, or correct in edge cases, and a developer who cannot read the underlying code may struggle to diagnose problems, manage costs, or handle data responsibly. Reliance on copied instructions also means that when something breaks outside the model's suggestions, the user has limited fallback. The author's stated success appears to reflect genuinely working, published apps, but the long-term reliability of software produced this way is harder to judge from a single account.

Even with those reservations, the post is a useful data point on how the practice of building software is changing. It suggests that for simple, well-scoped projects, motivation and a willingness to iterate may now matter as much as formal coding knowledge or English fluency.

8063bddd418c47c5.bodyJa:
CSS Modules はクラス名の衝突を防ぎつつコンポーネント単位でスタイルを閉じ込められる仕組みとして、React や Next.js を中心に広く使われている。一方で VSCode 標準の IntelliSense は CSS Modules で定義したクラス名を補完候補として提示してくれないため、styles.xxx と書くたびに CSS ファイルを別タブで開いて確認する、という手間が生じやすい。今回紹介する typescript-plugin-css-modules は、この不便さを解消するための定番プラグインだ。

CSS Modules では、たとえば styles.module.css といったファイルに定義したクラスを import styles from './styles.module.css' のように読み込み、styles.button のかたちで参照する。このとき TypeScript から見ると styles は型情報を持たないオブジェクトに過ぎず、エディタはどんなクラス名が存在するかを知り得ない。結果として補完もタイプチェックも効かず、クラス名のタイプミスにも気づきにくい状態になる。

typescript-plugin-css-modules は TypeScript の Language Service Plugin として動作し、参照先の CSS ファイルを解析してクラス名を型として供給する。導入はパッケージをインストールしたうえで、tsconfig.json の compilerOptions に plugins として "typescript-plugin-css-modules" を追加するだけだ。加えて VSCode 側では、コマンドパレットから「TypeScript: Select TypeScript Version」を選び、ワークスペースのバージョンを使う設定にしておく必要がある点に注意したい。エディタ同梱の TypeScript ではプラグインが読み込まれないことがあるためだ。

この設定が効くと、styles. と打った時点で定義済みのクラス名が候補として並び、存在しないクラスを参照した場合は型エラーとして検出できるようになる。SCSS や Less を併用する構成にも対応しているとされ、設定ファイルで camelCase 変換などの挙動を調整できる。

同種の課題に対しては、ビルド時に .d.ts ファイルを生成する typed-css-modules のようなアプローチもある。また、Tailwind CSS のようにユーティリティクラスを直接記述するスタイリング手法や、CSS-in-JS を採用する場合は前提が異なるため、こうした補完の悩み自体が発生しにくい。プロジェクトのスタイリング方針に応じて、どの手段が開発体験を高めるかを比較検討する余地はあるだろう。
8063bddd418c47c5.bodyEn:
CSS Modules are a widely used technique for scoping styles in component-based JavaScript and TypeScript projects, yet Visual Studio Code does not, by default, offer autocompletion for the class names those modules expose. For developers who work with frameworks such as React, Vue, or Next.js, this gap can mean constantly switching between a component file and its stylesheet to remember exact class names, with typos surfacing only at runtime. A TypeScript language service plugin called typescript-plugin-css-modules addresses this by feeding class information into the editor's IntelliSense.

To understand why the plugin matters, it helps to recall how CSS Modules work. Instead of writing global CSS, a developer imports a stylesheet as an object, for example "import styles from './Button.module.css'", and then references individual rules through properties such as "styles.primary" or "styles.isActive". The build tooling rewrites those class names into unique, locally scoped identifiers, which prevents naming collisions across a large codebase. The trade-off is that the imported object is opaque to the editor: without extra type information, VSCode treats it as a generic module and cannot suggest which properties exist or warn when a name is misspelled.

The typescript-plugin-css-modules package closes that loop by parsing the referenced CSS, SCSS, or LESS files and generating type definitions on the fly. Once configured, the editor can list available class names as you type, surface errors for nonexistent classes, and support features like go-to-definition that jump from a usage in the component straight to the corresponding rule in the stylesheet. Because it operates as a TypeScript language service plugin rather than a separate extension, it integrates directly with the type checking that VSCode already performs.

Setup generally involves a few steps. The package is installed as a development dependency through a package manager such as npm, yarn, or pnpm. It is then registered in the project's tsconfig.json under the "plugins" entry inside "compilerOptions", typically as an object with the name "typescript-plugin-css-modules". The final and frequently overlooked step is telling VSCode to use the workspace version of TypeScript rather than the one bundled with the editor, since language service plugins only load when the workspace TypeScript is active. This is done through the "TypeScript: Select TypeScript Version" command or a corresponding setting in the workspace configuration. Projects that use preprocessors or custom naming conventions can adjust the plugin's options, for example to handle camelCase versus kebab-case class names.

It is worth noting the boundaries of what this approach provides. The plugin improves the editing experience inside the editor but does not itself bundle or transform CSS; the actual scoping is still handled by the build pipeline, whether that is Webpack with css-loader, Vite, or another toolchain. The two concerns are complementary, and a misconfiguration in either layer can still produce mismatches between what the editor suggests and what ships to the browser.

There are adjacent tools and alternatives worth comparing. Some developers generate explicit type declaration files for their CSS Modules using utilities like typed-css-modules or the typescript-react-css-modules family, which write ".d.ts" files to disk rather than computing types in memory. That approach can be more transparent and works outside the editor, but it requires keeping generated files in sync. Other extensions, such as CSS Modules-focused VSCode add-ons, offer navigation features without deep TypeScript integration. The choice often depends on whether a team prioritizes zero generated artifacts or wants type information that other tooling, including the command-line compiler, can also consume.

The broader context is a continued push to bring stronger type safety and editor assistance to styling, which has historically been weakly typed compared with application logic. Approaches like CSS-in-JS libraries, utility-first frameworks such as Tailwind CSS with its own IntelliSense extension, and typed CSS Modules all attempt to reduce the friction of referencing styles correctly. For teams that have already committed to CSS Modules, adding typescript-plugin-css-modules is a relatively low-cost change that can reduce context switching and catch a class of errors earlier. As always, verifying the current configuration syntax against the plugin's documentation is advisable, since setup details and option names can change between versions.

caec66ca855d4cf7.bodyJa:
GitHub Copilotの課金体系が見直されたことを機に、LLM（大規模言語モデル）が消費するトークンをいかに抑えるかが、日常的にAIコーディング支援を使う開発者の現実的な関心事になりつつある。本記事は、その節約を支えるオープンソースのツール群を整理し、選び方の観点を示すものだ。

背景にあるのは、Copilotが従来の定額に加え、高性能モデルの利用回数を「プレミアムリクエスト」として数える仕組みを導入した点だ。プランごとに月間の割り当てが定められ、超過分は追加課金される設計とされる。AnthropicのClaude CodeやCursorなど競合ツールも、利用量やモデルに応じた従量課金の比重を高めており、トークン量がそのままコストに直結しやすい状況が広がっている。

ここで鍵になるのが、AIに渡す文脈（コンテキスト）の量だ。リポジトリ全体や長い会話履歴を無造作に送ると、トークンは膨らみやすい。そこで、必要なファイルや情報だけを選別して渡す、いわゆるトークン効率化の発想が重要になる。

その実装手段として注目されるのが、MCP（Model Context Protocol）に対応したツールだ。MCPはAnthropicが公開した、AIモデルと外部データやツールを標準化された方式で接続する仕組みで、対応サーバーを介して必要な情報だけを動的に取得できる。これにより、あらかじめ大量の文脈を詰め込まずに済む可能性がある。

OSSを選ぶ際の観点としては、対応するエディタやCLIとの相性、コンテキストの絞り込み精度、トークン消費量やログを可視化できるか、メンテナンスの活発さなどが挙げられる。ツールによって得意分野は異なるため、自分の利用スタイルに合うかを小さく試すのが現実的だろう。

課金改定は負担増と受け取られがちだが、利用量を意識する契機にもなる。トークン効率化のツールは万能ではないものの、コストと品質のバランスを取る選択肢として、今後さらに整備が進む可能性がある。
caec66ca855d4cf7.bodyEn:
GitHub's move to revise how Copilot is billed has pushed many developers to look more closely at how many tokens their AI coding assistants actually consume. As pricing shifts from flat monthly fees toward models that count "premium requests" or meter usage against underlying large language models, the cost of an interactive coding session is no longer fixed. For teams that run agents, call external tools, or feed large context windows into models all day, small inefficiencies can compound into noticeable monthly bills. That economic pressure is the backdrop for a growing category of open-source software aimed at reducing token consumption without sacrificing output quality.

The core issue is that modern AI development workflows are token-hungry by design. Tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code increasingly operate as agents that read files, search repositories, run commands, and reason over the results in multiple turns. Each turn re-sends context, and the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, has made it easy to attach external data sources and tools to a model. MCP is an open standard that lets an assistant connect to servers exposing files, APIs, or databases in a consistent way. The convenience is real, but every tool description, schema, and intermediate result that an MCP server returns is counted as input or output tokens. A verbose server or an over-broad context strategy can quietly inflate usage.

Against this background, several classes of open-source tools have emerged. One group focuses on context pruning and retrieval, sending the model only the most relevant files or code snippets rather than entire directories. These typically rely on embeddings and vector search to rank what matters for a given query, an approach often described as retrieval-augmented generation. A second group targets prompt and response compression, summarizing long histories, trimming redundant boilerplate, or caching repeated context so it does not need to be re-sent. A third group works at the MCP layer itself, acting as proxies or gateways that filter, batch, or shorten the tool outputs before they reach the model. The shared goal across all of them is fewer tokens per useful result.

Choosing among these tools depends less on raw feature lists and more on where the waste actually occurs in a given workflow. Developers evaluating options would do well to measure first, since most assistants and APIs expose token counts per request. If the bulk of tokens comes from large file context, retrieval and chunking tools are likely to help most. If costs stem from long, multi-turn agent sessions, history summarization or prompt caching may matter more. When MCP servers are the culprit, a filtering proxy or a leaner server implementation could be the better fit. Other practical considerations include how a tool integrates with existing editors and CLIs, whether it supports the specific models in use, the licensing terms, and how actively the project is maintained, since this space is moving quickly and many projects are still early.

It is worth noting that token efficiency is not solely a third-party concern. Model providers have introduced their own mechanisms, such as prompt caching that discounts repeated context and smaller, cheaper model tiers intended for routine tasks. Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have published guidance on structuring prompts to take advantage of these features, and some of the savings available through OSS tooling overlap with capabilities now built into the platforms. Developers should therefore weigh whether an external tool adds meaningful savings beyond what the provider already offers, and whether the added complexity is justified.

There are trade-offs to keep in mind. Aggressive context trimming or summarization can remove information the model needed, leading to weaker answers and, ironically, more follow-up requests. Compression and proxy layers add latency and another component to maintain. The most reliable approach appears to be incremental: establish a baseline of current token usage, apply one optimization at a time, and confirm that output quality holds. The billing revision that prompted this scrutiny is, in that sense, a useful forcing function. It encourages developers to understand what their AI tools are actually doing under the hood, which tends to produce leaner, more predictable workflows regardless of how any single vendor chooses to price its service in the future.

228c0c483506cd5a.bodyJa:
Cursor が自社開発するエージェント向けモデル「Composer」の更新版「Composer 2.5」が注目を集めている。今回取り上げる Zenn のブログ記事は、Anthropic の Claude Code や OpenAI の Codex を併用する開発者が抱きやすい不満を起点に、Composer 2.5 がもたらすとされる三つの利点を整理したものだ。

前提として、Cursor は VS Code をベースにした AI コードエディタで、複数の大規模言語モデルを切り替えながら使える点に特徴がある。Composer はその中でも Cursor が独自に手がけるモデルで、対話の往復を重ねながらコードを編集していく「エージェント的」な作業を、できるだけ速くこなすことを狙って設計されているとされる。Cursor 2.0 と合わせて投入された経緯があり、2.5 はその改良版という位置づけと見られる。

記事が挙げる一つ目の利点は、応答の速さだ。生成までの待ち時間が短くなれば思考が途切れにくく、集中を保ったまま実装を進めやすくなる。「返答が遅くて集中が切れた」という体験は、対話型のコーディングでは無視できない負担になりやすい。

二つ目は、利用上限への不安が和らぐ点だとされる。AI コーディングツールでは、トークン量や回数の制限、従量課金が気になって思い切って使えないという声が少なくない。Composer 2.5 がコストや上限の面で扱いやすくなっていれば、試行錯誤のハードルは下がる可能性がある。

三つ目は、結果の確からしさだ。時間をかけて生成させても結局動かず、やり直しになるという失敗は珍しくない。一度で意図どおり動く確率が高まれば手戻りが減り、体感の生産性は大きく変わり得る。

もっとも、これらの利点は作業内容やコードベースの規模によって感じ方が異なる。Claude や GPT 系のモデルも改良が続いており、どのモデルが最適かは一概には言えない。Cursor のようにモデルを使い分けられる環境では、タスクごとに比較しながら選ぶ姿勢が現実的だろう。
228c0c483506cd5a.bodyEn:
Composer 2.5 is the latest iteration of Cursor's in-house coding model, and for developers who spend most of their day inside an AI-assisted editor, the update is pitched directly at the friction points that tend to break concentration during long sessions. The original blog post frames the appeal around three practical benefits, each addressing a complaint that will sound familiar to anyone who has worked with agentic coding tools such as Anthropic's Claude Code or OpenAI's Codex.

The first benefit is speed. The post's central argument is that slow responses are not just an inconvenience but a productivity drain: while waiting for a model to think and generate, the developer's attention drifts and the mental thread of the task is lost. Composer is Cursor's own model, and the company has positioned it as a system optimized for low latency in agentic workflows rather than purely for maximum reasoning depth. Composer 2.5 appears to continue that direction, prioritizing responsiveness so that edits, file searches, and multi-step actions return quickly enough to keep a developer in flow. For iterative work, where a coder makes dozens of small requests in an hour, even modest latency reductions can compound into a meaningfully smoother experience.

The second benefit concerns usage limits and predictability. The blog post describes the anxiety of working against rate caps or token budgets, only half-joking that worrying about limits can keep you up at night. This is a real consideration with premium frontier models, where heavy agentic use can consume quotas quickly and force users to ration their requests. Because Composer is developed and served by Cursor itself, the company has more control over how it prices and meters the model, which the author suggests translates into a more relaxed allowance for everyday use. Readers should treat exact limit figures as subject to change, since Cursor's plans and quotas have been revised several times, but the general point is that running a first-party model can reduce the cost pressure that comes with routing every request to an external provider.

The third benefit is reliability, or the likelihood that generated code actually works the first time. The post highlights the frustration of spending significant effort on a task only to find the output does not run, requiring another round of prompting and correction. Composer 2.5 is presented as more dependable on this front, producing changes that are more likely to be correct and complete within a single pass. This claim is harder to verify objectively, since results vary by language, codebase, and prompt quality, so it is best read as the author's impression rather than a measured benchmark. Still, the underlying logic is sound: a model tuned specifically for the editing and tool-use patterns of an agentic IDE may handle that environment more consistently than a general-purpose model adapted to it.

Some background helps situate these claims. Cursor is a code editor built on a fork of Visual Studio Code, and it has increasingly moved toward agentic features where the assistant plans, edits, and runs multi-step tasks with limited supervision. Composer represents the company's strategy of building its own models alongside offering access to third-party options like Claude and GPT-series models, giving it a way to control latency, cost, and behavior end to end. That mirrors a wider industry trend in which coding-tool vendors blend proprietary and partner models. Claude Code, a terminal-based agent from Anthropic, and Codex, OpenAI's coding agent, are the natural comparison points the post invokes, since both are strong on reasoning but depend on their providers' infrastructure and pricing.

The practical takeaway is that Composer 2.5's value proposition is less about topping reasoning leaderboards and more about the everyday ergonomics of AI-assisted coding: faster turnarounds, fewer worries about hitting limits, and more first-try success. Whether those advantages hold for any given workflow will depend on the user's stack and habits, so the most reliable test is direct comparison on real tasks. As with any rapidly evolving tool, specific performance and pricing details are likely to shift, and readers should confirm current figures against Cursor's official documentation.

c017c41462dfb232.bodyJa:
VSCodeの統合ターミナルが、同じリモート環境にSSH接続しているにもかかわらず片方のPCだけ極端に重い——そんな現象の原因が、アクセシビリティ設定の「Screen Reader: yes」だったという事例が共有された。Claude Codeのように出力量の多いツールを使う際、クライアント側の描画モードが体感速度を大きく左右することを示す好例だ。

報告によれば、二台のPCから同一のリモートサーバーへSSHで接続し、VSCodeの統合ターミナル上でClaude Codeを動かしていたところ、片方のPCだけスクロールやテキスト描画が著しく遅かったという。リモート側の環境やコマンドは共通であるため、原因はクライアント側、つまりVSCodeの描画処理にあると見られる。

VSCodeの統合ターミナルは、内部的にWebベースのターミナルエミュレータ「xterm.js」を採用している。描画方式にはWebGL、Canvas、DOMといった複数のレンダラーがあり、通常はGPUを活用するWebGLやCanvasによって高速に文字を描画する。ところが、スクリーンリーダーが有効と判定されると、VSCodeは支援技術が内容を読み取れるようDOMベースの描画へ切り替える。この方式は要素を逐一HTMLとして生成するため、大量の文字が高速に流れる場面では負荷が高くなりやすい。

今回「犯人」とされたのは、この「Screen Reader Optimized」モードだったという。VSCodeにはアクセシビリティ設定「editor.accessibilitySupport」があり、既定値の「auto」ではOS側のスクリーンリーダーの起動を自動検知して最適化モードへ移行する。何らかの理由で、この検知が片方のPCだけ有効になっていた可能性がある。

対処としては、スクリーンリーダーを実際には使っていない場合、この設定を「off」にすることでGPU描画が復帰し、体感速度の改善が期待できる。コマンドパレットから「Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode」を実行する方法もある。

この事例は、ターミナルの体感速度がサーバー性能やネットワークだけでなく、クライアント側の描画モードに強く依存することを改めて示している。AIエージェント型のコーディング支援ツールが普及し、ターミナルへの出力が増えるなかで、描画性能の最適化は今後さらに重要になる可能性がある。一方で、アクセシビリティ機能は視覚障害のある利用者にとって不可欠であり、安易に無効化を勧めるのではなく、必要性に応じて切り替える姿勢が望ましい。
c017c41462dfb232.bodyEn:
A developer recently documented a frustrating but instructive performance problem: Visual Studio Code's integrated terminal felt noticeably sluggish on one computer while running smoothly on another, even though both machines connected to the same remote server over SSH and ran the same workload. The slowdown was most visible when using Claude Code, Anthropic's command-line coding assistant, whose verbose, frequently updating output made the lag impossible to ignore. After ruling out network latency and remote-side resource limits, the writer traced the cause to a single editor setting: screen reader mode, reported internally as "Screen Reader: yes."

The reason this matters goes beyond a one-off annoyance. VSCode's terminal performance depends heavily on how text is rendered, and screen reader mode changes that rendering path in ways that are easy to overlook. Understanding the mechanism helps explain why two otherwise identical setups can behave so differently.

By default, the integrated terminal is built on xterm.js and uses a GPU-accelerated renderer, typically WebGL, to draw characters quickly. This lets the terminal repaint large volumes of scrolling output with minimal CPU cost. When VSCode believes a screen reader is active, however, it switches the terminal into an accessibility-oriented mode. In that mode the editor exposes terminal contents through the DOM so assistive technology can read them, and it limits the visible buffer to a smaller number of lines. The trade-off is that this DOM-based approach is far less efficient than GPU rendering, so rapid output and scrolling can become heavy and unresponsive.

The subtle part is how the setting gets enabled in the first place. VSCode's "editor.accessibilitySupport" option defaults to "auto," which means the editor tries to detect whether a screen reader is running on the host operating system. That detection is not always accurate. It appears to be triggerable by accessibility services, certain background utilities, or a previous manual toggle, and once it latches on, the editor keeps screen reader mode active without any obvious indication. Because the detection runs on the local machine, a remote SSH session does not change the outcome, which is likely why only one of the two PCs was affected while both shared the same server environment.

Confirming the state is straightforward. The Command Palette includes a "Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode" command, and VSCode can display the current status. Setting "editor.accessibilitySupport" explicitly to "off" disables the behavior, while "on" forces it for users who actually rely on assistive technology. Restoring GPU rendering generally returns the terminal to its normal speed. Separately, the terminal exposes "terminal.integrated.gpuAcceleration," which controls whether WebGL or canvas rendering is used; if performance problems persist, that setting is another place to check, though it is distinct from the accessibility path.

This case is a useful reminder that perceived terminal performance is really a rendering problem, not just a shell or network problem. Tools like Claude Code, along with other agentic CLIs built around large language models, tend to stream long, continuously refreshing output, including progress indicators and reflowed text. That pattern stresses the renderer far more than typing a few commands does, so a rendering fallback that would be unnoticeable in light use becomes painful here. The same dynamic appears with other heavy terminal workloads, such as tailing large logs or running build tools with rich console output.

For anyone chasing similar slowdowns, a practical order of checks is to compare the two environments rather than assume the remote side is at fault, verify the accessibility setting, and then look at GPU acceleration and any GPU driver issues on the local machine. It is also worth noting that VSCode has invested in terminal performance over several releases, including the WebGL renderer and ongoing accessibility improvements, so the goal is not to disable accessibility features broadly but to ensure they are active only when intended. In this instance the fix was simple once the cause was clear, but the diagnostic path, eliminating the network and the server before suspecting a local editor setting, is the part most likely to help others facing an unexplained difference between two machines.

0020f768bfb6b03b.bodyJa:
VSCodeの統合ターミナルで長いログやコマンドの実行結果を流すと、少し前の出力がスクロールしても見つからなくなることがある。多くの場合、原因はターミナルが画面外に保持できる行数の上限にあり、設定を見直すことで改善できる可能性が高い。開発中にビルドログやテスト結果をさかのぼって確認したい場面では、地味に困る問題だ。

VSCodeのターミナルは内部的にxterm.jsというブラウザ向けのターミナルエミュレータを利用しており、画面外にスクロールして残せる行数(スクロールバック)には上限が設けられている。この上限を超える出力があると、古い行から順に破棄されていくため、いくらスクロールしても消えた部分は戻ってこない。該当する設定はterminal.integrated.scrollbackで、既定値は1000行とされている。長大なログを一度に出力するツールを使う場合、この行数はすぐに埋まってしまう。

対処としては、設定(settings.json)でterminal.integrated.scrollbackの値を引き上げる方法が分かりやすい。たとえば10000などに増やせば、より多くの履歴を保持できる。ただし、保持する行数を増やすほどメモリ使用量が増える点には注意が必要で、極端に大きな値を設定すると動作が重くなる可能性がある。用途に応じて適度な値に調整するとよい。

根本的に履歴を失いたくない場合は、ターミナルの行数に頼らず、出力をファイルへ書き出す方法も有効だ。コマンドの末尾にリダイレクトを付けたり、teeコマンドを併用したりすれば、画面表示とは別に全文をファイルへ残せる。確認時はlessなどのページャで開けば、行数の制限を気にせずさかのぼれる。

なお、こうしたスクロールバックの上限はVSCode固有の制約ではなく、Windows TerminalやiTerm2といった他のターミナルにも同様の設定が存在する。出力が途中で切れていると感じたときは、まず利用しているターミナルのバッファ設定を確認するのが定石と言える。ログ量が多い開発では、設定の調整とファイル出力を組み合わせておくと安心だろう。
0020f768bfb6b03b.bodyEn:
Developers who rely on Visual Studio Code's integrated terminal occasionally find that long build logs, test output, or the results of earlier commands vanish from view and cannot be recovered by scrolling upward. This can be disruptive during debugging, because the very lines that explain a failure are often the ones that have already scrolled out of reach. Understanding why it happens, and which settings control it, makes the terminal a more dependable tool for everyday work.

The most common cause is the terminal's scrollback buffer limit. VSCode's integrated terminal retains only a fixed number of lines in memory, controlled by the setting terminal.integrated.scrollback. By default this value is 1000, which means that once a command produces more than roughly a thousand lines of output, the oldest lines are discarded to make room for new ones. The text is not hidden somewhere; it has been dropped from the buffer entirely, so scrolling back simply reaches the top of what remains. For verbose tooling such as compilers, package managers, or test runners, exceeding a thousand lines is easy, which is why the truncation appears to happen so often.

The direct fix is to raise the scrollback limit. This can be done through the Settings UI by searching for "scrollback," or by editing settings.json directly and adding a line such as "terminal.integrated.scrollback": 10000. A larger number keeps more history available, and setting it to a very high value retains a great deal of output. The trade-off is memory usage: each retained line consumes resources, and an extremely large buffer can increase the editor's memory footprint and, in some cases, affect rendering performance. Choosing a value that comfortably covers typical command output, rather than the maximum possible, is usually a reasonable balance.

A second, related cause appears when the window is reloaded or the session is restored. VSCode can persist terminal sessions across reloads through terminal.integrated.enablePersistentSessions, but the amount of history that is restored is governed separately by terminal.integrated.persistentSessionScrollback. This value defaults to a smaller number, so even if the live scrollback limit is high, a reopened terminal may show only a fraction of the earlier output. If history seems to shrink specifically after closing and reopening VSCode, this setting is the likely factor and can be increased as well.

Beyond configuration, it is worth recognizing that the scrollback buffer is inherently a finite, in-memory store and not a substitute for durable logging. For output that genuinely needs to be preserved, redirecting it to a file is more robust. Appending an operator such as > output.log captures standard output, while piping through the tee command writes to a file and still prints to the screen at the same time. The resulting file can then be opened in the editor, searched, and kept for later reference without depending on the terminal's memory. Paging tools such as less or more are another option for stepping through long output interactively without losing earlier sections.

Some apparent truncation has a different origin altogether. Commands that draw progress bars or status lines frequently use carriage returns to overwrite the same line in place, so what looks like missing history is actually intended single-line behavior. Similarly, programs that detect a non-interactive context may alter how much they print. These cases are distinct from the buffer limit and are not resolved by changing scrollback settings.

For context, the integrated terminal is built on xterm.js, the same terminal emulator component used by several other editors and tools, and its buffering model is broadly comparable across them. Standalone terminal emulators expose similar scrollback options, so the underlying concept transfers if a workflow moves outside VSCode. The practical takeaway is that disappearing terminal output is generally expected behavior driven by a configurable limit rather than a defect. Raising terminal.integrated.scrollback, adjusting persistent session scrollback when reloads are involved, and writing important output to files together address the great majority of cases where logs or command history appear to be cut off.

0dcdc9ed83e7a319.bodyJa:
ローカルLLMの活用において、外部知識をどう与えるかは精度と速度を左右する重要な設計判断だ。本記事は、検索で関連文書を都度引いてくるRAG（Retrieval-Augmented Generation）と、知識をあらかじめモデルの文脈に読み込ませて使い回すCAG（Cache-Augmented Generation）を、同一条件で比較した「実測・結果編」にあたる。

前提となるのは両者の根本的な違いだ。RAGはベクトル検索などで質問に関連する断片だけを取り出してプロンプトに差し込む。文書量が膨大でも必要な部分だけを渡せる一方、検索の的中精度がそのまま回答品質に響く。対するCAGは、対象となる知識全体を一度コンテキストに入れて推論し、その際に計算されるKVキャッシュ（プレフィックスキャッシュ）を保存・再利用する。二回目以降は長い前置きの再計算を省けるため、検索処理を挟まずに応答できる可能性がある。

検証は、同じLLM、同じ50問、同じ採点者という条件をそろえ、「知識の渡し方」だけを変える設計で行われたという。変数を一つに絞ることで、速度と精度の差がどちらの方式に由来するかを切り分けやすくなる。特にプレフィックスキャッシュの効果を手元の環境で計測している点は、理論値ではなく実機の挙動を確かめるうえで参考になる。

背景には、長文コンテキストを扱えるモデルの普及がある。コンテキスト窓が広がったことで、知識をまるごと詰め込むCAG的な発想が現実味を帯びてきた。llama.cppやvLLMといった推論基盤はプレフィックスキャッシュやKVキャッシュの再利用に対応しつつあり、ローカル環境でも同種の最適化を試しやすくなっている。

ただし、両者は優劣を競うというより適材適所と見るのが妥当だろう。知識が頻繁に更新される、あるいは文書総量がコンテキスト窓を大きく超える用途ではRAGが扱いやすい。一方で、知識が固定的で何度も同じ参照を行う用途では、CAGが速度面で有利になる場合があると考えられる。今回のような実測は、こうした使い分けの判断材料を増やすものとして意義がある。
0dcdc9ed83e7a319.bodyEn:
Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG) has emerged as a lightweight alternative to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for grounding local large language models in private knowledge, and a recent hands-on benchmark set out to measure whether it can actually compete on speed and accuracy. As the follow-up to an earlier implementation walkthrough, this results-focused report pits the two approaches against each other under deliberately controlled conditions: the same local model, the same 50 questions, and the same automated grader. The only variable is how the relevant knowledge reaches the model.

The comparison matters because RAG and CAG solve the same problem in fundamentally different ways. RAG keeps a document corpus outside the model, converts both documents and the incoming query into embeddings, retrieves the most relevant chunks from a vector store, and injects them into the prompt at inference time.
