記事でいう「経営OS」とは、特定の製品を指すのではなく、受発注管理や見積作成、顧客対応、経理処理といった日常業務をスクリプトやワークフローとして束ね、AIが横断的に扱えるようにした自作の仕組みを指すと見られる。既製の業務ツールを個別に使うのではなく、自社の商流に合わせて手続きをコード化することで、3人という規模でも作業の抜け漏れや引き継ぎコストを抑えられるという考え方だ。

背景には、生成AIの実務適用が「文章を書く」段階から「業務そのものを動かす」段階へ移りつつある流れがある。近年はAIエージェントに複数ステップの作業を任せる動きが広がり、外部ツールと連携する仕組みとしてMCP（Model Context Protocol）なども登場している。こうした要素を組み合わせれば、専任のエンジニアを多数抱えなくても、小さなチームが自前の自動化基盤を持てる余地が生まれつつある。

一方で、この構成をそのまま再現できるかは、業種や取引の複雑さ、担当者のリテラシーに左右される部分が大きい。AIが生成した処理の検証体制や、機密情報の取り扱い、外部APIのコスト管理といった運用面の課題も残る。月商という指標も事業の実態を必ずしも表さないため、数字だけを一般化するのは慎重であるべきだろう。

それでも、少人数チームがAIを核に業務を再設計する試みは、人手不足に直面する多くの小規模事業にとって示唆に富む。個別の成功事例をどこまで自社に取り込めるかを見極めながら、段階的に検証していく姿勢が求められそうだ。
67d9dcf34710ee8d.bodyEn:
A three-person company has published an account of building its own "AI management operating system" using Claude Code, Anthropic's command-line coding agent, to run a business generating roughly ¥2.5 million (around $16,000) in monthly revenue. The report matters because it illustrates a growing pattern: very small teams using agentic AI tools not only to write software, but to automate the operational plumbing that once required additional staff or a stack of paid SaaS subscriptions.

The phrase "AI management OS" here does not describe a formal product but a bespoke collection of scripts, integrations, and automated workflows the team assembled to coordinate daily operations. In practice, systems of this kind typically tie together tasks such as invoicing, customer communication, scheduling, reporting, and data entry, with an AI layer handling routine decisions and drafting. Because the team is only three people, the appeal is straightforward: automating repetitive work lets each member concentrate on higher-value activities while keeping fixed costs low.

Claude Code sits at the center of the described setup. Released by Anthropic as a terminal-based agentic tool, it can read and edit files, run commands, and iterate on tasks with limited human supervision, which makes it well suited to building and maintaining internal tooling. Unlike a chatbot that only returns text, Claude Code operates directly in a developer's environment, allowing a small team to prototype custom automations quickly rather than commissioning bespoke software or manually stitching together multiple vendor platforms.

Technically, arrangements like this often rely on connecting the agent to existing services through APIs and, increasingly, the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard Anthropic introduced to let AI models interact with external tools and data sources in a structured way. This enables an agent to pull information from spreadsheets, databases, or third-party apps and then act on it. The article appears to emphasize practical, 2026-era workflows, which suggests the team has iterated on its system as the underlying models and tooling matured over time.

The broader context is a wave of interest in AI-augmented small businesses and micro-team operations. Adjacent tools compete for similar attention: editor-based assistants such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot target code authoring, while automation platforms like Zapier, Make, and the open-source n8n focus on connecting apps without heavy programming. What distinguishes an approach built around Claude Code is the degree of flexibility, since a capable agent can generate and revise custom logic rather than relying on predefined connectors. That flexibility comes at the cost of needing someone to specify, review, and maintain what the agent produces.

It is worth treating any single case study with appropriate caution. The ¥2.5 million monthly figure reflects one company's specific market, product, and margins, and the same tooling would not guarantee comparable results elsewhere. Building and maintaining custom automation also requires enough technical literacy to supervise an AI agent, review its output, and handle failures gracefully—skills that are not universal among small-business operators. Reliability, security, and the handling of sensitive customer data are recurring concerns whenever AI agents are granted access to live operational systems, and these risks likely grow as more of a business is entrusted to automated processes.

For readers considering a similar path, a few prerequisites tend to matter. Comfort working in a terminal, a basic understanding of APIs and version control, and a willingness to start with narrow, low-risk automations before expanding scope all appear to reduce friction. Keeping a human in the loop for financial actions and customer-facing messages is a common safeguard, as is maintaining logs so that an agent's decisions can be audited after the fact.

Taken together, the account is a useful data point in an emerging conversation about how far small teams can stretch with agentic AI. It does not prove that a three-person structure is optimal or broadly replicable, but it does document a concrete workflow that others can examine and adapt. As models, MCP integrations, and agent tooling continue to evolve, similar reports are likely to become more common, and comparing them will help clarify which practices genuinely scale down to the smallest of organizations and which remain specific to a particular team's circumstances.

dc96ce35820f010b.bodyJa:
Anthropic の CLI ツール「Claude Code」で、意図せず起動するビルトインスキルを設定ファイル CLAUDE.md によって抑制する手法が注目されている。開発者がセッション中に呼び出されるツールを細かく制御できる点で、実務での使い勝手に直結するテーマだ。

Claude Code はターミナル上で動作する AI コーディング支援ツールで、コードの読み書きやファイル操作、テスト実行などをエージェント的にこなす。近年はあらかじめ用意された「ビルトインスキル」によって、特定の状況で自動的に機能が呼び出される仕組みが備わっている。これによって定型作業を省力化できる一方、開発者の意図とは異なるタイミングでツールが起動し、想定外の挙動につながる場面もあると指摘されている。

今回紹介されている手法は、プロジェクトのルートなどに置く CLAUDE.md にディレクティブ（指示文）を記述し、特定スキルの自動起動を抑える、というものだ。CLAUDE.md は Claude Code が起動時に読み込むメモリファイルで、コーディング規約やプロジェクト固有の前提、使ってほしくないコマンドなどを自然言語で書いておくと、モデルがその文脈を踏まえて動作する。ここに「このスキルは自動で使わない」といった趣旨の指示を明記することで、不要なツール呼び出しを減らせる可能性がある。

背景には、AI エージェントの自律性と制御性のバランスという課題がある。自動化が進むほど作業は速くなるが、レビューや意図の反映が難しくなる場面も出てくる。CLAUDE.md による制御は、プロジェクト単位で振る舞いを明文化できるため、チーム内で挙動を共有しやすい利点があると見られる。

ただし、CLAUDE.md はあくまで自然言語による指示であり、設定ファイルのような厳密な強制力を持つとは限らない。モデルのバージョンや文脈次第で従わないケースもあり得るため、重要な制約は権限設定や確認プロンプトなど他の仕組みと併用するのが無難だろう。同種の課題は他社のエージェント型ツールでも議論されており、指示の粒度と再現性をどう担保するかは、今後の共通テーマになりそうだ。
dc96ce35820f010b.bodyEn:
Claude Code, Anthropic's agentic command-line tool for software development, ships with a set of built-in skills that can trigger automatically when the model judges them relevant to a task. That convenience becomes a problem when a skill fires unexpectedly, altering a session's behavior in ways the developer did not intend. This article describes a technique, discussed in a recent Qiita post, for suppressing that automatic activation by writing explicit directives into the CLAUDE.md configuration file, giving teams finer control over which tools run during a session.

Built-in skills are packaged capabilities that extend what the assistant can do beyond plain code generation, such as handling particular file formats, running specific workflows, or invoking helper routines. Because they are designed to activate contextually, Claude Code may decide on its own that a skill matches the current request and invoke it without an explicit instruction. In many cases this is helpful, but in constrained or reproducible workflows an unexpected tool call can introduce noise, consume tokens, change files, or produce output that diverges from what a developer expected. The core issue the article addresses is predictability: when automation decides for you, the result is harder to reason about.

The proposed solution leans on CLAUDE.md, the project-level context file that Claude Code reads at the start of a session and treats as persistent guidance. CLAUDE.md is commonly used to record coding conventions, architectural notes, commands to run tests, and other project-specific instructions. Because its contents are injected into the model's working context, it also functions as a place to state behavioral constraints. The article's approach is to add explicit directives instructing the assistant not to auto-invoke certain built-in skills, effectively converting an implicit, model-driven decision into an explicit, developer-defined rule. In practice this means naming the skills or behaviors to avoid and phrasing the instruction clearly enough that the model treats it as a hard constraint rather than a soft preference.

It is worth being precise about what this method does and does not guarantee. Instructions placed in CLAUDE.md shape the model's behavior through natural-language guidance rather than a hard configuration switch, so the outcome is influenced by how the model interprets the directive. This appears to work reliably for many cases, but it is likely to be less absolute than a formal permission system. Developers who need stronger guarantees should be aware that CLAUDE.md guidance and structured settings serve different purposes, and combining both tends to produce the most consistent results.

That distinction connects to adjacent controls in the Claude Code ecosystem. The tool also supports a settings file, often referenced as settings.json, where permissions for tools and actions can be allowed or denied more formally, and where behavior can be scoped at the user, project, or enterprise level. For teams integrating external capabilities, the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, defines how additional tools and data sources are exposed to the assistant, and those integrations carry their own permission considerations. Anthropic has also promoted the broader idea of Agent Skills as a way to package reusable expertise, which makes understanding activation control increasingly relevant as more skills become available.

The wider context is a maturing conversation about controllability in agentic coding tools. As assistants gain the ability to act autonomously, editing files, running commands, and calling tools, developers increasingly want deterministic, auditable behavior, especially in continuous integration pipelines, shared repositories, or regulated environments where an unexpected action carries real cost. Competing and complementary tools, including editor-integrated assistants and other CLI agents, face the same tension between helpful automation and predictable output. Techniques like the one described here reflect a general pattern: using a project's context file as a lightweight governance layer.

For readers wanting to apply this, the prerequisites are modest. You need a working Claude Code installation and a CLAUDE.md file at the project root or in a location the tool recognizes. From there, the article suggests documenting which skills should remain dormant and testing the configuration by running representative tasks to confirm the unwanted activations no longer occur. Because model behavior can shift across versions, it is prudent to revalidate such directives after updates and to treat CLAUDE.md as living documentation. Used thoughtfully, this approach offers a practical way to keep automation on a shorter leash without giving up the productivity that built-in skills can provide.

935c55a079fd5d76.bodyJa:
初めてiOSアプリを開発する未経験者が、AIコードエディタ「Cursor」を相棒に、わずか1週間でベータテストの公開まで到達したという体験記が公開された。AIを活用したペアプログラミングが、初心者の開発速度を大きく引き上げ得ることを示す事例として注目される。

Cursorは、VS Codeをベースに開発されたAI統合型のコードエディタで、自然言語での指示に基づくコード生成や修正、既存コードの説明などを対話的に行える点が特徴だ。エラーメッセージを貼り付ければ原因の推定と修正案を提示したり、プロジェクト全体の文脈を踏まえた提案を返したりする機能を備える。こうした「AIとの協働」は、文法やフレームワークの知識が不足しがちな初学者にとって、学習と実装を同時に進められる利点があると見られる。

一方で、iOSアプリ開発には固有の前提知識が求められる。プログラミング言語のSwiftやUIフレームワークのSwiftUI、そしてAppleの統合開発環境Xcodeの操作、さらにベータ配信に使うTestFlightの仕組みなど、習得すべき要素は少なくない。今回の体験記は、これらの学習コストをAIが部分的に肩代わりすることで、短期間でも動くアプリを形にできる可能性を示している。

AIによるコーディング支援の分野では、GitHubのCopilotをはじめ、AnthropicのClaudeやOpenAIのモデルを組み込んだツールが相次いで登場しており、競争が激化している。CursorはこれらのモデルをAPI経由で利用しつつ、コードベース全体を横断的に扱える編集体験を打ち出している。単なる補完にとどまらず、複数ファイルにまたがる変更を一括で提案する点が、従来のエディタとの差別化要素とされる。

ただし、AIが生成したコードをそのまま採用することにはリスクも伴う。誤った実装やセキュリティ上の問題を見抜けないまま公開してしまう懸念があり、最終的な品質担保には人間によるレビューやテストが欠かせない。今回のような成功事例は、あくまでAIを補助輪として使いこなす姿勢と、公開前の検証を怠らない前提の上に成り立つものと言えそうだ。個人開発の敷居が下がりつつある現状を象徴する一例として、参考になる部分は多いだろう。
935c55a079fd5d76.bodyEn:
A recently published personal account describes how a developer with no prior iOS experience used Cursor, an AI-assisted code editor, as a coding companion to build an app and reach a beta testing release within a single week. The story matters because it illustrates a broader shift in how newcomers approach software development, suggesting that AI pair programming can meaningfully lower the barrier to entry for platforms that have traditionally demanded significant upfront learning.

Native iOS development typically involves a steep initial climb. Newcomers must become comfortable with Swift, Apple's modern programming language, and increasingly with SwiftUI, the declarative framework for building interfaces. They also need to navigate Xcode, Apple's integrated development environment, and understand platform-specific concepts such as the app lifecycle, provisioning profiles, code signing, and the requirements of the App Store review process. For someone starting from zero, assembling all of these pieces can take weeks or months before a working app is ready to share.

The account attributes the compressed timeline largely to the role Cursor played as a constant collaborator. Cursor is a code editor built on a fork of Visual Studio Code that integrates large language models directly into the coding workflow. It offers features such as inline code generation, chat-based assistance that can reference the current codebase, and the ability to apply multi-file edits from natural language instructions. For a beginner, this appears to function like an always-available mentor, explaining unfamiliar Swift syntax, proposing implementations, and helping diagnose errors without requiring the developer to leave the editor or search external documentation for every question.

According to the author's framing, the value of this setup was not simply that the AI wrote code, but that it accelerated the learning loop. When an error appeared, the developer could ask for an explanation and a fix in context, then iterate quickly. This kind of tight feedback cycle is likely one of the reasons a first-time developer could progress from concept to a testable build so rapidly. It is worth noting, however, that reaching a beta is a meaningful milestone but not the same as shipping a polished, production-ready product. Beta releases are intended precisely to surface bugs, usability issues, and edge cases that early development can miss.

For iOS specifically, distributing a beta usually means using TestFlight, Apple's official service for inviting testers to try pre-release builds. Getting there still requires enrollment in the Apple Developer Program, which carries an annual fee, along with correctly configured signing and an App Store Connect record. These steps are administrative rather than purely technical, and an AI assistant can help explain them, but the underlying accounts, approvals, and platform rules remain the developer's responsibility. Readers considering a similar path should factor in this overhead alongside the coding work itself.

Cursor sits within a fast-moving category of AI-assisted development tools. Adjacent options include GitHub Copilot, which pioneered mainstream inline code completion, as well as newer entrants and editor integrations from various vendors. The underlying models often come from providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI, and the competitive pace means capabilities and pricing change frequently. This context helps explain why individual experience reports like this one are appearing more often: the tools have matured to the point where non-specialists can attempt projects that once seemed out of reach.

Some caveats deserve emphasis. AI-generated code can be plausible but incorrect, may follow outdated patterns, or can introduce security and privacy issues that a beginner might not recognize. Relying heavily on generated solutions can also leave gaps in fundamental understanding, which tends to matter more as an app grows in complexity. Experienced practitioners generally recommend treating AI output as a draft to be reviewed rather than an authoritative answer, and this guidance seems especially relevant for someone learning a platform for the first time.

Taken together, the account is best read as an encouraging but individual data point rather than a guarantee of results. It suggests that with a clear goal, a manageable scope, and an AI collaborator handling much of the boilerplate and explanation, a motivated newcomer can move from idea to beta unusually quickly. The durability of that progress, and the quality of the final product, will likely depend on how much the developer continues to build genuine expertise alongside the assistance the tools provide.

e9ffccd5ad3c3c42.bodyJa:
GitHub は、Copilot の使用状況メトリクスレポートについて、データの精度とカバレッジを改善したと発表した。組織が Copilot の導入状況や実際の利用実態をより正確かつ網羅的に把握できるようになるもので、エンタープライズ規模で生成 AI を活用する企業にとって、投資効果を評価するうえでの基盤強化となる。

使用状況メトリクスとは、Copilot がどの程度アクティブに利用されているか、コード補完やチャット機能がどれだけ受け入れられているか、どのプログラミング言語やチーム、ユーザー層で使われているかといった指標を集約したものだ。GitHub は組織や Enterprise の管理者向けにこうしたデータを提供しており、REST API や管理画面のレポートを通じて確認できる。今回の更新では、こうした集計値の精度が高まり、これまで反映が不十分だった利用のケースがより広くカバーされると見られる。

背景には、Copilot の機能が急速に拡張してきた事情がある。当初はエディター上のコード補完が中心だったが、現在では Copilot Chat、プルリクエストの要約、コマンドライン向けの支援、さらにエージェント的な機能まで対象が広がっている。機能が多様化するほど、単一の指標では利用実態をとらえきれなくなるため、計測の網羅性を確保することが課題となっていた。今回の改善は、こうした多面的な利用を漏れなく数値化する方向性に沿ったものと言える。

企業にとって、この種のメトリクスは単なる稼働状況の確認にとどまらない。ライセンス費用に見合う効果が出ているか、どのチームで定着が進んでいるか、逆に活用が進まない部門はどこかといった判断材料になる。生成 AI コーディング支援の分野では、GitLab Duo や Amazon Q Developer など競合も利用分析機能の拡充を進めており、導入効果を可視化する仕組みは各社の差別化要素になりつつある。

管理者は、レポートの数値が以前と比べて変動する可能性がある点に留意したい。精度向上に伴い過去の傾向と数値が変わる場合もあるため、時系列で比較する際は改善の適用時期を踏まえて解釈することが望ましいだろう。
e9ffccd5ad3c3c42.bodyEn:
GitHub has rolled out improvements to the accuracy and coverage of its Copilot usage metrics reports, giving organizations a more dependable and complete picture of how the AI coding assistant is being adopted and used across their teams. For enterprises that have invested in Copilot at scale, reliable measurement is central to justifying spend, refining rollout strategies, and understanding where the tool delivers the most value, so improvements to the underlying data quality directly affect how administrators make those decisions.

The changes focus on two related dimensions. The first is accuracy, meaning the reported figures more faithfully reflect the actual activity taking place, reducing discrepancies that could previously arise from gaps in data collection or inconsistent aggregation. The second is coverage, meaning the reports capture a broader and more representative range of the interactions and users that make up an organization's Copilot footprint. Taken together, the update is intended to reduce the risk that administrators draw conclusions from incomplete or under-counted data.

Copilot usage metrics are typically surfaced through the organization and enterprise admin experiences, as well as through GitHub's Copilot metrics API, which lets customers pull structured usage data into their own dashboards and reporting pipelines. These metrics generally include indicators such as the number of active and engaged users, suggestion activity, acceptance behavior, and usage broken down across features like code completions and Copilot Chat. When the accuracy and coverage of the source data improve, everything built on top of it, including custom analytics, internal adoption scorecards, and third-party reporting integrations, is likely to benefit as well.

For large organizations, the practical implications are significant. Adoption analytics are frequently used to identify teams that are actively engaged versus those that have licenses but low activity, information that helps administrators reallocate seats, target enablement efforts, and estimate return on investment. If underlying counts were previously undercounting engaged users or omitting certain activity, decisions about license renewals or expansion could have been based on a conservative or skewed view. More comprehensive coverage appears intended to give a fuller account of real-world usage, which can matter when Copilot spend is being reviewed against measurable outcomes.

This update fits into a broader pattern in which GitHub has steadily expanded the administrative and observability tooling around Copilot. Over the past few product cycles, GitHub has introduced and refined the Copilot metrics API, added more granular breakdowns of feature usage, and provided enterprise controls for policy management and access. The emphasis on measurement reflects the reality that AI coding assistants have moved from experimental pilots to standard parts of many development workflows, and that budget owners increasingly expect the same level of usage reporting they get from other enterprise software.

It is worth noting the distinction between usage metrics and productivity outcomes. Metrics such as active users and suggestion acceptance describe engagement with the tool, but they do not by themselves prove downstream effects like faster delivery or higher code quality. Organizations often combine Copilot usage data with their own engineering metrics, developer surveys, or frameworks such as DORA and SPACE to build a more rounded assessment. Improved accuracy in the raw usage numbers strengthens that foundation, but interpretation still requires care, and correlation between adoption and performance should not be assumed to be causation.

Administrators who rely on these reports may want to review recent trends after the change takes effect, since improved coverage could cause reported figures to shift compared with earlier periods. A rise in counts, for example, may reflect better measurement rather than a genuine change in behavior, so historical comparisons that span the update should be interpreted with that context in mind. Teams that ingest data through the metrics API may also want to confirm that their pipelines and dashboards handle any resulting changes consistently.

As published in the GitHub changelog, the update is presented as a data quality enhancement rather than a change to features or pricing, and it applies to the existing reporting surfaces organizations already use. For customers evaluating or scaling Copilot, the net effect is a more trustworthy basis for the adoption and usage conversations that increasingly accompany enterprise AI tooling, and a reminder that measurement infrastructure is becoming as important as the assistant features themselves.

0f329052fb62bd17.bodyJa:
大規模言語モデル（LLM）の推論を大規模に運用するうえで、KVキャッシュのメモリ管理は大きな課題となっている。Google Cloudは公式ブログで、コンテナ基盤のGKE（Google Kubernetes Engine）と並列ファイルシステムのManaged Lustreを組み合わせ、このKVキャッシュを複数ノードにオフロードするアーキテクチャを公開した。長いコンテキスト長や高スループットが求められる推論ワークロードを、実用的な規模でスケールさせる狙いがある。

KVキャッシュとは、Transformerが文章を生成する際に、過去のトークンに対する注意（アテンション）計算の中間結果であるKeyとValueを保持する仕組みを指す。これにより毎回同じ計算を繰り返さずに済むが、キャッシュのサイズはコンテキスト長やバッチサイズに比例して増大する。GPUやアクセラレータの高帯域メモリ（HBM）は容量が限られ高価なため、長文処理や多数の同時リクエストではメモリが逼迫し、再計算（プリフィル）によるコスト増や遅延が生じやすい。

今回のアプローチは、HBMに収めきれないKVキャッシュを、より大容量で低コストな外部ストレージ層へ退避させる考え方に基づく。Managed LustreはHPC向けに設計された高性能な並列ファイルシステムで、低レイテンシと高い集約帯域を特徴とする。GKE上で稼働する推論エンジンから複数ノードにまたがってキャッシュを共有・再利用できるようにすることで、同一プロンプトの前方部分を使い回すプレフィックスキャッシュなどの効果を、単一ノードの枠を超えて発揮させられる可能性がある。

背景には推論エンジン側の進化がある。vLLMなどのオープンソース実装ではPagedAttentionによる効率的なメモリ管理が普及し、KVキャッシュを階層的に退避するLMCacheのような仕組みも広がりつつある。NVIDIAもDynamoなどでキャッシュの分散管理を進めており、KVキャッシュのオフロードは推論最適化の共通テーマになりつつある。

この構成は、Geminiのような長文対応モデルを自社環境で高スループットに提供したい事業者にとって、アクセラレータメモリの制約を緩和する選択肢となり得る。ただし実際の効果はモデルやワークロード、ネットワーク構成に依存するため、導入時にはストレージ帯域とアクセラレータ利用効率のバランスを検証することが重要と見られる。
0f329052fb62bd17.bodyEn:
Google Cloud has published a technical walkthrough describing how to scale large language model inference by offloading the key-value (KV) cache across multiple nodes, combining Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with Google Cloud Managed Lustre. The approach targets a growing constraint in production LLM serving: as context windows lengthen and request volumes rise, the memory needed to hold KV cache data can exceed the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) available on accelerators, which caps throughput and raises cost per token.

The KV cache is central to efficient text generation in transformer models. During autoregressive decoding, a model would otherwise recompute the attention keys and values for every prior token at each new step. Caching those tensors avoids the repeated work, but the cache grows roughly in proportion to sequence length and batch size. For long-context workloads spanning tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, the cache can occupy a large share of accelerator memory, leaving less room for concurrent requests and larger batches. When memory runs short, servers typically evict cache entries and later recompute them, which increases latency, especially the time to first token.

The pattern outlined in the post moves KV cache data off the accelerator into a shared, high-performance storage tier rather than discarding it. This reflects a tiered memory hierarchy that descends from HBM to host DRAM, local SSD, and networked storage. Managed Lustre, Google Cloud's managed implementation of the Lustre parallel file system widely used in high-performance computing, provides the networked layer. Because it offers high aggregate throughput and low latency across many clients, it appears well suited to storing and reloading large cache blocks quickly. The critical detail is that the store is shared: cache produced on one node can be read by another, so a request routed to a different server can reuse previously computed state instead of running the prefill phase again.

That multi-node sharing is what makes the design notable. In a single-node setup, prefix caching only helps when a later request lands on the same server that holds the relevant cache. Placing the cache in a common Lustre file system raises the effective cache hit rate across a fleet, which is particularly valuable for workloads with repeated system prompts, shared documents, or long conversational histories. GKE handles orchestration, scheduling inference pods, mounting the shared file system, and scaling the serving layer, while the storage tier decouples cache capacity from the memory of any individual node.

The technique sits alongside a broader industry effort to manage KV cache more intelligently. Inference engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM already implement prefix caching and CPU offloading, and projects like LMCache focus specifically on storing and retrieving KV cache across tiers and machines. NVIDIA's Dynamo framework similarly emphasizes distributed KV cache management for disaggregated serving. Commercially, prompt or context caching features from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google's own Gemini API expose related savings to developers by charging less for reused context. The GKE and Managed Lustre combination is best understood as an infrastructure-level way to implement these ideas at scale on Google Cloud.

Several prerequisites shape whether the approach pays off. Offloading only helps when the cost of writing and reading cache over the network is lower than recomputing it on the accelerator, so the ratio of reused tokens to fresh tokens matters, as does the bandwidth between compute nodes and storage. Very large batch sizes, long shared prefixes, and high request concurrency tend to favor offloading, whereas short, unique prompts may see little benefit. Teams evaluating the pattern will likely want to measure time to first token, tokens per second, and cache hit rates against a baseline that keeps everything in HBM.

More broadly, the post illustrates how storage and networking are becoming first-class concerns in LLM serving, not just accelerator count. As models push toward longer contexts and agentic workflows that carry extensive state, the ability to persist and share intermediate computation across a cluster is likely to remain an active area of optimization, with parallel file systems, object storage, and specialized cache tiers each playing a role.

9c6f346430372edb.bodyJa:
Googleは、機械学習開発者向けの新たな選択肢として、Google Cloud WorkbenchのVS Code拡張機能を正式公開した。この拡張機能により、エンジニアは使い慣れたローカルのVS Code環境を離れることなく、Google Cloudの高性能なコンピューティングリソースを活用したML開発が可能になる。

Workbenchは、Vertex AIの一部として提供されるマネージドな開発環境で、GPUやTPUを含むスケーラブルな計算資源をノートブック形式で利用できる点が特徴だ。従来、こうしたクラウド上の計算環境を使う場合、ブラウザベースのJupyterLabや専用インターフェースへ切り替える必要があり、ローカルの開発ツールとの間で作業が分断されがちだった。今回の拡張機能は、VS Codeのリモート開発機能を土台に、クラウド上のWorkbenchインスタンスへ接続し、その計算資源上でコードの実行やワークロードの管理を行える仕組みと見られる。

開発者にとっての利点は、環境の切り替えが不要になる点にある。普段利用している拡張機能、キーバインド、Gitとの連携、デバッガーといったVS Codeのエコシステムをそのまま活かしながら、大規模なモデル学習やデータ処理をクラウド側に任せられる。ローカルマシンのスペックに縛られずに済むため、ラップトップからでも大規模な計算を伴う実験を回しやすくなる可能性がある。

背景には、ML開発ワークフローをいかに開発者の日常に溶け込ませるかという競争がある。GoogleはColab EnterpriseやVertex AIを通じてクラウドMLの裾野を広げてきたが、多くのエンジニアが日常的に使うIDEはVS Codeであるという現実がある。同様の発想は他社にも見られ、AWSのSageMaker StudioやMicrosoftのAzure Machine Learningも、VS Codeとの統合やリモート接続機能を強化してきた。IDEを起点にクラウドの計算資源へシームレスに橋渡しする流れは、業界全体の潮流と言える。

生成AIの普及に伴い、モデルの学習やファインチューニングに求められる計算資源は増大している。ローカルとクラウドの境界を意識せずに開発できる環境は、こうした需要に応えるうえで重要度を増しそうだ。実際の使い勝手や対応するインスタンス構成、課金体系については、利用を検討する際に公式ドキュメントで確認することが望ましい。
9c6f346430372edb.bodyEn:
Google Cloud has released a Workbench extension for Visual Studio Code, giving machine learning engineers a way to run and manage training and experimentation workloads on Google Cloud infrastructure without leaving their local editor. The move matters because it targets one of the most persistent frictions in ML development: the constant switching between a comfortable local coding environment and a separate browser-based or cloud console interface where the heavy compute actually lives.

At its core, the extension connects VS Code to Vertex AI Workbench, Google Cloud's managed Jupyter-based environment for data science and machine learning. Rather than opening a hosted notebook in a browser tab, developers can attach their existing VS Code installation to a Workbench instance and use Google Cloud's compute resources, including high-performance CPUs, GPUs, and potentially TPUs, as the backend for their work. This means code editing, debugging, extensions, keyboard shortcuts, and version-control integration remain in the familiar IDE, while the computation runs on remote managed hardware.

The appeal is largely about workflow continuity. ML practitioners typically prototype on a laptop, then move to more powerful machines for training on large datasets or models that exceed local memory and accelerator limits. Historically that transition has required re-establishing the environment, re-uploading code, or working through a web notebook that lacks the tooling many engineers rely on. By keeping a single editor as the constant, the extension aims to reduce that overhead. Google frames the benefit as eliminating environment switching, which is likely to appeal to teams that already standardize on VS Code across their organization.

Technically, the approach appears to build on VS Code's established remote development capabilities. VS Code has long supported connecting to remote machines, containers, and Windows Subsystem for Linux through its Remote Development extensions, where the editor runs locally but the language server, terminal, and execution happen elsewhere. A Workbench extension that follows this model would let the local client stay lightweight while offloading compute to Google Cloud. It also fits with the broader industry pattern of meeting developers inside the tools they already use rather than pushing them toward proprietary web consoles.

For context, Vertex AI is Google Cloud's unified platform for building, training, and deploying machine learning models, and Workbench is its notebook-centric entry point. Around it sits a wider ecosystem that includes Vertex AI training pipelines, model registries, feature stores, and endpoints for serving. The extension is best understood as a client-side convenience layer over these services rather than a new compute product in itself. Given the Gemini category and Google's current direction, it is reasonable to expect tightening integration between this tooling and Google's AI models over time, though the primary value proposition described here is infrastructure access and developer experience.

The release also lands in a competitive space. Amazon offers the AWS Toolkit for VS Code alongside SageMaker Studio and its own code editor experiences, while Microsoft ships an Azure Machine Learning extension for VS Code that similarly bridges local editing with cloud compute. Cloud-agnostic and hosted options such as JupyterLab, GitHub Codespaces, and various managed notebook services compete for the same users. In that light, Google's move can be read as table stakes for a major cloud provider: making sure that engineers who prefer VS Code, one of the most widely adopted editors, have a first-party path onto the platform.

Prospective users should keep a few practical considerations in mind. Running workloads on Google Cloud compute incurs the usual billing for the underlying instances and accelerators, so the extension does not change the cost model of the resources it connects to. Authentication typically depends on Google Cloud credentials and appropriate Identity and Access Management permissions, and performance for interactive work can be sensitive to network latency between the local client and the remote instance. Teams evaluating the tool will likely want to confirm how it handles session persistence, environment reproducibility, and data governance for sensitive datasets.

Overall, the Workbench extension is an incremental but meaningful addition that reflects a clear trend toward integrated, local-first developer tooling for cloud-based machine learning. For engineers already invested in both VS Code and Google Cloud, it appears to lower a real barrier, and its longer-term significance will depend on how deeply it integrates with the rest of the Vertex AI stack.

44e0601e54730b8d.bodyJa:
Google は、AI エージェント開発フレームワーク「Agent Development Kit（ADK）」の大型アップデートとなる ADK 2.0 を公開した。マルチエージェントシステムを支えるコアアーキテクチャを刷新し、本番環境で信頼性の高いエージェントをより効率的に構築・展開できるようにした点が今回の主眼とされる。

ADK は、複数のエージェントが協調してタスクを分担・実行する「マルチエージェント」構成を前提に設計されたフレームワークである。単一の大規模言語モデルに一問一答で応答させるのではなく、役割の異なるエージェントを組み合わせて複雑な処理を段階的にこなす方式は、近年のエージェント開発における主要な潮流となっている。ADK 2.0 では、こうしたエージェント間の連携や状態管理、実行制御といった土台部分の設計が見直されたと説明されている。

刷新の狙いは、いわゆる「プロダクション対応（production-ready）」の強化にあるとみられる。試作段階では動作するエージェントも、実運用では処理の再現性や障害時の挙動、監視・デバッグのしやすさといった課題に直面しやすい。コアアーキテクチャを再構築することで、こうした信頼性や運用性の面を底上げする意図があると考えられる。

背景には、AI エージェント分野での開発競争の激化がある。OpenAI や Anthropic がエージェント構築向けの SDK やツールを整備し、オープンソースでも LangChain／LangGraph、Microsoft の AutoGen、CrewAI といった選択肢が広がっている。Google 自身も、Gemini モデル群や、エージェントを運用基盤に載せる Vertex AI 側の仕組みと組み合わせる形での提供が想定される。ADK はエージェント間連携の標準化を進める Agent2Agent（A2A）などの取り組みとも関連づけられてきた。

開発者にとって、フレームワークのメジャー改訂は既存コードの移行やベストプラクティスの見直しを伴う可能性がある。実際の使い勝手や安定性は、今後のドキュメント整備とコミュニティでの検証を通じて明らかになっていくとみられる。
44e0601e54730b8d.bodyEn:
Google has released version 2.0 of its Agent Development Kit (ADK), the open-source framework it offers to help developers build and coordinate AI agents. The company frames the release as a significant rethink rather than an incremental update, saying it re-architects the toolkit's core foundations so that multi-agent systems can be built and deployed more reliably in production. That focus matters because many teams have found it comparatively easy to demonstrate a single capable agent, yet much harder to run several cooperating agents dependably at scale.

ADK originally launched in 2025 as part of a broader Google effort to give developers a structured approach to agent building, moving beyond one-off prompt engineering toward reusable components and defined orchestration patterns. The framework is designed to pair closely with Gemini models while remaining largely model-agnostic, and it centers on concepts such as tools, agent delegation, session state, and workflows that route tasks between specialized agents. By describing 2.0 as a foundational overhaul, Google appears to be signaling that the earlier architecture reached practical limits as applications grew more complex and long-running.

The reasons Google gives for rebuilding the core tend to cluster around reliability and predictability. In multi-agent setups, small inconsistencies in how state is tracked, how errors propagate, or how control passes between agents can compound into unpredictable behavior. A rearchitected foundation is likely intended to make these interactions more observable and controllable, giving developers clearer authority over how agents hand off work, share context, and recover when a step fails. Improvements in these areas would also make agent behavior easier to test and debug, which is a common obstacle when moving from a prototype to a supported service.

Production readiness is the other theme running through the release. Deploying agents involves more than model calls; it requires evaluation, monitoring, versioning, and integration with existing infrastructure. Google has positioned ADK to work with its managed runtime, Vertex AI Agent Engine, which handles deployment, scaling, and operational concerns on Google Cloud. A cleaner core architecture in ADK 2.0 would, in principle, make the path from local development to managed deployment smoother, though the practical gains will depend on how existing projects migrate and whether the new design introduces breaking changes.

ADK does not exist in isolation. It sits alongside a growing set of open standards and competing frameworks that reflect intense industry interest in agentic systems. Google has promoted the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol for communication between agents built by different teams or vendors, and the broader ecosystem has coalesced around the Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic, for connecting models to external tools and data. Rival frameworks such as LangChain's LangGraph, CrewAI, Microsoft's AutoGen, and OpenAI's Agents SDK pursue similar goals with different design philosophies, so ADK 2.0 can be read partly as Google's response to a fast-moving and still-unsettled category.
